This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for approximating the principal eigenfunction of the Laplacian in domains of n-dimensional real or complex Euclidean space. To address the challenge of numerical solutions being dependent on specific architectures and datasets, we employ the methods of modern neural networks and apply theoretical insights from the analysis of neural networks to understand the relationship between potential solutions. Notably, our results demonstrate the generalization performance to be robust against changes in the architecture of the neural networks without assuming uniform smoothness of the target function. Furthermore, our findings are substantiated by a range of numerical experiments. The research presented here can be seen as an extension of the work of the authors on the approximation of the Dirichlet problem in [SIAM J. Math. Data Sci. 3, no. 2, 2021]. This method views text as a collection of interconnected concepts, utilizing a relation-based knowledge graph to capture relationships between individual words and the broader context. An explicit memory of article information is maintained, allowing for the incorporation of new words and updating existing knowledge, ultimately enabling a more comprehensive understanding of text through a procedural Inference Module that applies domain-specific rules to draw out implicit meaning. Unlike traditional machine learning methods, this method eschews training in favor of a direct transfer of text information into the declarative memory, accompanied by an inference process that leverages the interconnections within the knowledge graph to distill the most significant information from text. An evaluation of the method's performance using the Wikipedia dataset demonstrated that it could accurately identify the most crucial article information across various domains, even when exposed for the first time, effectively showcasing its ability to learn and adapt from text through a combination of declarative memory and inference. Furthermore, the method's text representation capabilities were found to be versatile in real-world applications, such as question answering, as evidenced by its 100% accuracy in answering 20 questions about the articles it had previously encountered. This method's potential for knowledge acquisition and transfer was also highlighted by its ability to recognize and differentiate between synonymous concepts, as well as its capacity for generalization, allowing it to apply its knowledge to novel articles and domain-specific questions. Overall, the method's performance in these tasks underscores its potential as a pioneering AI system grounded in cognitive psychology, capable of distilling the most essential information from text and leveraging that information to drive its decision-making processes. We provide explicit equations for the cosine term in a modified version of Chebyshev polynomials. This leads to a factorization of the form $u^2 - 2av_1 + (a^2 - b^2) = (x - \cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})) (x^2 + ax + b)$. From the given equations, we derive an efficient method for factoring third-degree polynomials of the form $x^3 + p x^2 + q x + r$. This method has a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\log^2 d)$. Additionally, we show that a modified version of Chebyshev polynomials, denoted as $T_{2^{\frac{\log d-1}{k}-1}(x)$, can be used for factoring $d$-nomials in the form of $u^2 - 2av_1 + (a^2 - b^2) = T_{2^{\frac{\log d-1}{k}-1}(x)$. This factorization is applicable to any integer $k \ge 2$ and any integer $d$ divisible by an odd number and a power of two. This paper generalizes previous work on factoring third-degree and fourth-degree polynomials, specifically those of the form $x^3 = \cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$ and $x^4 + p x^2 + q x + r$, originally presented in [E. Berberi, M. F. Fesikh, Factoring variants of Chebyshev polynomials with minimal equations of $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$, J. Unconv. Math., 2020, 35, 1-15]. Our factorization has been implemented in SAGE and Maple. The SAGE implementation has a time complexity of $\mathcal{T}(N) = \mathcal{O}(\log^2 N \log d)$ and the Maple implementation has a time complexity of $\mathcal{T}(N) = \mathcal{O}(\log^3 N \log d)$. In this research, we investigate the issue of multi-group broadcasting in millimeter wave communication systems. To address this problem, we propose a novel hybrid encoding strategy that incorporates cycled and layered transmission methods. Specifically, cycled transmission involves cycling information bits, while layered transmission involves grouping information bits into multiple sublayers with varying lengths. By optimizing both cycled and layered transmission, we formulate a mixed-integer non-linear programming problem. A subproblem decomposition-based algorithm is then developed to solve this problem efficiently. Notably, this approach not only reduces computation time but also provides a tighter lower bound and faster convergence compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we present an initialization method to enhance algorithm performance. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our proposed algorithm through comprehensive simulations. Results indicate that the new hybrid encoding strategy outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of spectral efficiency and power efficiency. Notably, when cycled and layered transmission methods are both active, we observe nearly optimal performance with only a 1% loss in spectral efficiency and 2% loss in power efficiency compared to the optimal hybrid encoding strategy. Moreover, when cycled transmission is used exclusively, we observe a significant 60% reduction in power efficiency loss, while layered transmission incurs a 10% reduction in spectral efficiency loss. Additionally, we observe that the proposed algorithm consistently outperforms existing methods as the number of groups increases. Finally, we note that the performance gap between the proposed algorithm and other methods is more pronounced in scenarios with a large number of groups, highlighting the importance of hybrid encoding in these situations. The increasing prevalence of imprecise and incomplete data poses significant challenges for accurate decision-making, particularly when working with large datasets. Traditional approaches to decision support have relied heavily on decision tables, a method of structuring data that is widely accepted due to its clarity and simplicity. However, decision tables are not universally applicable and can be time-consuming and costly to generate from other data formats. To address these issues, we propose the concept of decision schemata, a comprehensive framework that encompasses decision tables along with other formats such as decision trees and Bayesian networks. A decision schema is a structured outline that includes specific fields, aiming to provide a unified understanding of decision support models. In the field of prototype-based learning, traditional methods rely on the assumption that prototypes are representative of their respective classes. However, when dealing with diverse and complex data sets featuring multiple sub-classes, this assumption often proves flawed. As a result, prototypes constructed from sample data tend to suffer from significant biases toward specific sub-classes, ultimately hindering overall performance. To address this challenge, we propose the Capsule Prototype Network (CPN), an innovative framework designed to capture class-type-specific prototypes. By integrating a capsule module, CPN effectively learns to identify and represent inherent sub-class patterns, thereby enhancing the accuracy of prototypes and boosting the overall performance of models. Experimental evaluations on multiple public datasets validate the efficacy of the proposed CPN method. Notably, on the datasets 'VehicleData', 'CUB-200-2011', and 'Stanford Online Organism Dataset', results demonstrate that CPN surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks by significant margins, with improvement rates of 11.0%, 8.2%, and 6.1%, respectively. Furthermore, CPN exhibits superior performance on datasets featuring multiple sub-classes, with performance gains of 10.0% and 8.1% observed on the 'VehicleData' and 'CUB-200-2011' datasets, respectively. As such, CPN represents a pioneering approach in prototype-based learning, particularly effective when dealing with datasets characterized by multiple sub-classes. Notably, the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques even when trained on limited data, with performance remaining stable under varying data scarcity conditions. Ultimately, the proposed method exhibits robust generalizability and versatility, with successful applications across multiple scenarios. This study proposes a novel ground-and-sky sensor network, dubbed Ground&Sky Net (GSSN), comprising sensors situated on the ground and above ground, working in tandem to augment and complement each other's capabilities. Given the geographical separation of these sensors, they are unable to communicate directly. To overcome this challenge, a wireless backhaul link is suggested to link the ground-level sensors to aerial sensors, such as High Altitude Platforms (HAPs), thereby enabling data transfer to a central control center. To address this multi-hop connectivity issue, a new algorithm, the Wireless Connection Algorithm (WCA), is designed to optimize the assignment of wireless connections between ground-level sensors and HAPs, with the goal of ensuring full network coverage and maximizing network scalability by minimizing the number of HAPs required. By formulating this problem as a Mixed-Integer Non-Convex Co-Optimization problem, WCA leverages an iterative optimization strategy to solve this problem and determine the optimal HAP assignment for each ground-level sensor. Furthermore, WCA incorporates a new metric, the "connection quality," to evaluate the suitability of HAPs for assignment based on their coverage area and positioning. Using simulation results, the effectiveness of WCA is demonstrated, and its advantages over existing solutions are highlighted. Specifically, WCA is shown to achieve better results, with a 30% lower number of HAPs required and a 25% lower interference level under various test scenarios. The proposed Ground&Sky Net architecture is envisioned to play a pivotal role in the development of future wireless communication systems, with its design and optimization providing valuable insights and lessons for the next-generation aerial-toterrain and aerial-to-ground wireless communication systems. This paper presents MoDeRNN, a novel approach to capturing dynamic properties of a subject's motion, by proposing an innovative RNN model that integrates past and current subject state information to forecast the subject's future position relative to other individuals involved in the interaction. The method involves an innovative RNN framework that utilizes a subject's integrated motion characteristics, including velocity, acceleration, and relative position, to forecast future interactions. To evaluate its efficacy, MoDeRNN was tested in two scenarios: (i) anticipating the direction of a subject's reach and (ii) forecasting a subject's intended target when carrying a load, utilizing a dataset known as ReachTarget. This research explores the performance and safety features of the Rust programming language's interoperability with other languages through the Foreign Function Interface (FFI). Investigating issues with data lifetime management, we identify specific challenges in handling temporary data objects. Building on this analysis, we propose a new framework, Josephine, that enhances FFI safety in Rust by improving garbage collection and temporal data management when working with foreign types. To demonstrate Josephine's effectiveness, we evaluate its impact on memory safety, performance, and developer safety. Results show that Josephine improves memory safety, decreases runtime and compilation times, and demonstrates the importance of proper type system management in cross-language programming. To facilitate further research, we provide open-source code examples on GitHub. Josephine has also been successfully implemented and tested in the Redline Steganographer project. In summary, our study shows that Rust's FFI can be improved through the optimization of local variable lifetime management, leading to notable gains in performance, safety, and developer productivity. The Josephine framework offers a concrete solution to address temporal data management, offering a safer and more efficient approach to cross-language programming. Cells possess a remarkable capacity for shape transformation, which is crucial in their adaptation to diverse environments. Currently, modeling cell forms is an intricate task mainly due to the irregularity of cellular surfaces and the scarcity of data in certain contexts. In this research, we introduce a novel method for representing cell shapes using implicit neural networks, which can efficiently handle non-planar surfaces and require only sparse reference points for training. To generate novel cell shapes, we employ a generator-network framework that combines a shape representation module with a GAN, allowing us to create imaginary cell surfaces through latent code manipulation. To evaluate our approach, we created a cell dataset with various species and applied it to two tasks: generating 3D cell volumes from cross-section images and creating imaginary cell surfaces based on real examples. The results indicate that our method outperforms existing techniques in generating 3D cell volumes and produces more realistic imaginary cell shapes when compared to other GAN-based approaches. The source code for this research will be publicly available upon publication. Moreover, we have developed a web-based interactive application that enables users to explore and understand the intricacies of our implicit neural representation model. This application can be accessed at https://cell-models.github.io/. Our research has the potential to contribute significantly to the creation of advanced computational cell models, which can be utilized in the development of artificial life forms and tissue engineering. It may also have implications in the diagnosis of rare diseases through AI-powered diagnosis. Ultimately, this research could pave the way for the development of creative modeling techniques to simulate and analyze the behavior of living cells and their potential applications in biotechnology and biomedicine. Furthermore, we have established a new research initiative focused on the development of artificial life forms and tissue engineering, which is detailed on our website at https://lifai.github.io/. We present XLNet, a unified pre-training model that surpasses RoBERTa in 1.4 language understanding tasks, while employing a generalized autoregressive pre-training method similar to BERT and BIDAF. Unlike BERT, XLNet avoids both monotonous pre-training objectives and information overlap in enhanced masking, while mimicking autoregressive language generation in enhanced masking objectives. Moreover, XLNet incorporates permutation-related objectives in pre-training and enhanced masking, which enables the model to capture deeper contextual and anti-masking dependencies. Our experimental results demonstrate that XLNet yields consistent improvements in language comprehension, and we specifically highlight its notable advancements in text classification, question answering, and natural language inference. Moreover, XLNet's pre-trained model and related code are publicly available at https://github.com/zhanghangyang/XLNet.pytorch. Our model also won the 2nd place in RepBERT track of RepGlue challenge at IJCAI 2020. With our model, the challenge organizers achieved state-of-the-art results in 12 language understanding tasks. The challenge code is publicly available at https://github.com/ruinzh/RepGlue. Let's assume these particles evolve according to a specific local time-correlated process, with a given characteristic speed and a potential function that determines this evolution. This process is referred to as a generalized diffusion. In this generalized diffusion, the mass of each particle affects its movement, with more massive particles experiencing a higher characteristic speed. We can relate this movement to a pure jump process, called a Q-process, based on the combined characteristics of the individual particles. We can show that a system of many particles evolving according to a specific rate matrix converges to the corresponding Q-process as the number of particles approaches infinity. This convergence is consistent across different numbers of particles, ensuring that the system still converges to the Q-process even in the limit as the number of particles approaches infinity. The performance of a dialogue system heavily relies on the subsequent speech recognition step, which significantly affects downstream tasks. Although speech recognition models provide confidence scores, their accuracy is often hindered by out-of-vocabulary words, mispronunciations, and poor audio quality, leading to uncertain transcriptions. To mitigate these issues, we propose refining the uncertainty quantification of automatic speech recognition (ASR) by leveraging the statistical distribution of recognition uncertainties. To this end, we introduce the concept of dialogue state monitoring as a downstream task to improve with ASR uncertainty modeling. By treating the ASR output as a sample from a language model, we generate a word confusion network (WCN) to represent the recognition uncertainty distribution. We then develop a dialogue state monitoring model that samples from the WCN to match the uncertainty distribution with the actual dialogue states. Experimental results on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset demonstrate that our proposed models outperform conventional ASR confidence scores in dialogue state monitoring tasks. Moreover, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach by integrating it with a slot tagging model, leading to enhanced performance on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset. Our method is further validated through ablation studies, highlighting the contributions of different components. The proposed model is expected to benefit downstream tasks by providing a more accurate understanding of ASR uncertainty, thereby enhancing the overall performance of dialogue systems. Continual learning research often overlooks a fundamental aspect: the requirement for continuous learning originates from real-world settings where data is typically obtained sequentially. This characteristic can be leveraged to implement straightforward strategies based on data freshness. Our primary goal is to assess the current reliance on large pre-trained models in the continual learning field and to introduce a basic approach that exploits the temporal ordering of data. Our results indicate that continual learning methods frequently underperform compared to a naive baseline that solely uses older data. Moreover, we observed that a simple method based on data freshness can approach the performance of state-of-the-art methods in several scenarios. Our research suggests that the application of expensive pre-trained models in continual learning should be reevaluated. Hate speech within social media is a pressing issue, encompassing not only text-based insults but also visual and auditory offenses. Existing hate speech identification models are predominantly text-based, often relying on machine learning techniques that analyze textual features. However, these models are susceptible to variations in linguistic and cultural contexts, hindering their performance outside of specific data sets. Furthermore, the methods used to train these models are shrouded in secrecy, making it impossible to gauge their reliability. To address these limitations, we propose a novel, text-to-image generation technique based on the MaLM-Art model, which produces hate speech-related images. We then develop and present a new understandingable hate speech identification model that integrates text and image modalities. This approach involves training a neural network to analyze the connections between text, image, and their combined sample, effectively mitigating the biases in individual modalities. We test our approach using data from the 2021 Hate Speech Identification track of the ODSC Europe 2021 competition, achieving superior results and demonstrating improved generalizability in cross-domain scenarios. Additionally, the proposed method allows for the visualization of the learned features through t-SNE analysis, while making the underlying training data and model architecture fully transparent. We further demonstrate the cross-modal generalization capabilities of our approach by training the model on social media hate speech data from German and evaluating it on Russian hate speech data, achieving a high F1 score of 0.755. We also conduct a thorough feature analysis across multiple data sets and discover that the learned features are consistent in terms of their semantic meaning. This breakthrough in hate speech identification through text-to-image synthesis opens up new avenues for multi-modal learning and understanding in NLP. We believe that the proposed approach can be adapted and applied to a wide range of natural language processing challenges, ultimately contributing to the advancement of NLP. The primary goal of model compression through knowledge distillation is to reduce the inference cost of a large, cumbersome model by replacing it with a smaller, less complex one that can achieve comparable accuracy. To accomplish this, the compressed model learns to mimic its larger counterpart's output probabilities. However, the compressed model's predictions may not match those of the large model when dealing with novel inputs, primarily because it cannot produce intermediate layer activations that are consistent with its larger counterpart due to differences in layer parameters. To address this limitation, the InDistill method introduces a novel distillation loss that preserves data flow by aligning the compressed model's intermediate outputs. This is achieved by modifying the compressed model to produce not only output probabilities but also class-specific inputs in the penultimate layer, which can then be regulated by the proposed distillation loss. By optimizing the compressed model under the proposed loss, the large model's intermediate outputs become more similar to those of the compressed model, enabling the compressed model to better replicate large model outputs. However, when given an adaptive choice of vectors (where the selection of each subsequent vector depends on the results of the previous ones), this algorithm fails to provide even a $(1+\epsilon)\lambda_{\max}$-approximation, even for the simplest scenario where the vectors are just successive integers. In this study, we show that CountSketch still provides an $(1+\epsilon)\lambda_{\max}$-approximation with high probability, but with a significantly increased running time of $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$, suggesting that the non-adaptive bound of $\sqrt{n}$ is the true space-optimal statistical limit for this problem. We also provide a more general negative result, stating that even with a much larger amount of space, say $n^{\delta}$ for any $\delta>0$, there still exists a family of vectors for which the $(1+\epsilon)\lambda_{\max}$-approximation cannot be achieved with high probability, except with an impractically large running time of at least $n^{\Omega(\delta^{-1})}$. This result has significant implications for other problems, such as finding the top-$k$ most frequent elements in a stream, where we show that the space-optimal statistical limit for this problem is $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{n})$. We also provide a more general characterization of the space-optimal statistical limit for this problem, stating that it is equal to $\Theta(n^{1/(2k+1)})$. This result holds even when the frequency of the elements can be estimated up to a small multiple of the mean frequency, rather than just an additive $\epsilon$-small quantity. Generating concise yet informative text is a crucial goal in natural language processing. To achieve this, we introduce an entity-optimization approach that enhances abstractive condensation by identifying and managing key entities in a text. To fine-tune entity understanding, we develop an entity-prompt learning framework that incorporates entity information into both source and target texts as masked words. An optimal entity configuration is then determined through planning to optimize text coherence and relevance. The resulting model demonstrates strong performance in text condensation and entity-related tasks, outperforming existing methods in various benchmarks. Notably, our entity-prompt learning framework can be integrated with existing generation models, such as the standard Transformer, without requiring significant model modifications. Furthermore, our planning strategy allows for adaptability across various generation models. The overall framework is denoted as Planning with Acquired Entity Prompts (PEPE). In the study of glaciology, researchers encounter a complex variational inequality associated with the Stokes equations, which arises from the free boundary problem of a two-dimensional ice sheet. This issue is particularly challenging due to the presence of a semicoercive constraint resulting from the ice's no-penetration condition. This paper presents a novel approach to resolving the partially coercive variational inequality using the finite element method, drawing inspiration from the continuous extension domain technique. To achieve this, we employ a continuous extension operator under the assumption of sufficient regularity, which we then apply to a discretized problem. However, we encounter difficulties in proving the convergence of the discrete operator, leading to the introduction of a new and general result applicable to a wide range of elliptic problems. Ultimately, we establish the convergence of a discrete extension operator, which in turn enables us to derive optimal convergence rates for the finite element approximation of the velocity and stress, as well as a convergence result for the stress tensor in the presence of a semicoercive constraint. This is accompanied by a thorough numerical illustration showcasing the method's efficiency. Research on the anisotropic triangular flow phenomenon in heavy-ion collisions at various energy levels has been conducted within the MPHARM theoretical framework. Calculations for $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 GeV were carried out for both gold and copper systems. It was discovered that the flow anisotropy exhibits energy-dependent properties, with a minimum value that correlates with specific energy levels. This behavior is comparable to that of the radial flow multiplicity $dN_{ch}/d\eta$. Furthermore, the flow anisotropy was found to be influenced by the number of participants in the collision, with participants on the starboard side exhibiting greater anisotropy than those on the port side. Additionally, the inclusion of string melting in the model results in reduced flow anisotropy, whereas the introduction of a flow resistance coefficient leads to anisotropy values that closely align with those of no flow resistance. This phenomenon suggests that the initial state of heavy-ion collisions at these energy levels lacks significant flow resistance. Lastly, the flow anisotropy was found to be insensitive to the initial spatial distribution of strings. This research provides a theoretical understanding of the physical mechanisms driving triangular flow and highlights its utility in gaining insights into the initial states of heavy-ion collisions. It also underscores the significance of further investigating the initial states of these collisions, with the potential to reveal new physics. This research may serve as a foundation for future investigations into the properties of exotic, multi-quark hadrons, with triangular flow offering a valuable diagnostic tool for probing these entities. It is envisioned that the MPHARM framework will play a vital role in this line of investigation. The integration of these robotic fingers enhances the system's stability and allows it to adapt to changing environments through dynamic movement. The evaluation of the robotic structure's stability before and after modification, as measured by its Lyapunov stability, confirms the benefits of this multi-functional design. The system's potential for space exploration has also been explored through a simulation study, assessing its ability to navigate and identify objects in microgravity environments. The system's performance in space was found to be comparable to that in ground-based experiments, validating its potential for use in space exploration missions. Research on spectral bias in neural networks suggests that as undertrained models
escalate errors, they may overfit and miss broader patterns in a dataset, leading to
poor predictions outside frequently seen examples. We investigated this phenomenon in
the context of Physics-Informed Neural Networks using the Van der Pol oscillator equation.
By undertraining these networks without momentum, we found they failed to generalize and
only provided accurate predictions at the training points, but when momentum was added,
even with reduced training epochs, these networks successfully generalized and produced
accurate predictions outside the training area, indicating momentum significantly
reduces the spectral bias effect in Physics-Informed Neural Networks. This discovery has
important implications for engineering and scientific research where precise generalization
is crucial, and potentially accelerates the application of PINNs in these fields. This
study reveals the potential of combining momentum with these networks to improve
generalization and provides valuable insights for future PINN research. This research was

This paper presents a novel Abstract Interpretation framework that integrates static analysis and static verification phases in a single, modular and flexible scheme. Traditional Abstract Interpretation methods conduct a single upward phase to approximate program regions, followed by a backward analysis to derive reachable state spaces. Our proposal, called the AB framework, separates these phases into distinct abstract domains, allowing them to be combined in various ways to optimize computation. By doing so, we can identify when the upward and backward phases can be merged or when they should remain separate, as in the AB$_2$$_B$ case, resulting in increased precision without additional computational cost. The proposed framework is supported by a comprehensive formal verification, and its practical effectiveness is demonstrated through case studies on modern programming languages, including contracts and concurrency features. AB's decoupling mechanism allows for the identification of scenarios where the upward and backward phases can be combined, leading to higher precision without additional computational cost in the AB$_2$$_B$ configuration. Additionally, our framework's flexibility enables the creation of hybrid configurations tailored to specific analysis needs. For instance, in the AB$_2$$_F$ configuration, featuring an expansive abstract domain, the upward phase can generate excessively large state spaces, necessitating a backward analysis with a more focused abstract domain to mitigate this issue. The AB framework's successful application in various contexts, including the analysis of Java bytecode, JavaScript, and Racket programs, as well as its open-source availability on GitHub, further validate its precision and performance benefits. Ultimately, our framework's modular design enables the seamless integration of new abstract domains, allowing for the adaptation of the AB framework to diverse analysis requirements. Review-based product recommendation is a crucial task for e-commerce platforms, where accurate sentiment analysis is vital for identifying relevant reviews and predicting product ratings.
A major drawback of current methods is that they blend positive and negative reviews equally, neglecting the distinct characteristics of sentiment-based word embeddings (wordvecks).
To address this limitation, we present the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), which interacts directly between review texts and wordvecks through cross-attention, allowing for the encoding of reviews using both sentiment-sensitive wordvecks and auto-encoded semantic features from the transformer's encoder.
The resulting review representations are then merged with product embeddings through a multi-modal attention mechanism, enabling the model to capture complex interactions between reviews and products.
Empirical evaluations on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of SIFN over state-of-the-art baselines, with the source code available on GitHub at https://github.com/whuwlxj/SIFN. Furthermore, an ablation study confirms the effectiveness of the proposed methods, while a wordveck analysis reveals interesting insights into the nature of wordvecks. The study also identifies instances of out-of-vocabulary words in wordvecks and reviews, highlighting potential avenues for further research. The study's findings are expected to contribute significantly to the development of sentiment-sensitive wordvecks and review-based product recommendation models. This paper investigates the feasibility of data augmentation in CSNLP for indigenous languages through a differential analysis of lexical substitution methods utilizing Arabic-English CS datasets. We found that employing CS words as substitutes outperformed using monolingual targets and control CS words as proxy monolingual expressions. Notably, our best-performing model trained with CS word substitutes achieved a 14.6% enhancement in accuracy over the baseline model. We also discovered that utilizing a parallel corpus to determine CS word substitutes yielded superior results (3.2% improvement) in comparison to randomly selecting substitutes. This study contributes to the understanding of data augmentation in CSNLP for indigenous languages and sheds light on its applications for low-resource settings. Hexahedral meshes have become the preferred choice for solving complex problems in science and engineering due to their ability to accurately represent boundary layers and irregular shapes. However, the advanced topologies of these meshes pose challenges for many existing algorithms, necessitating the development of new approaches that can efficiently operate on high-complexity hex meshes. Our research presents a comprehensive survey of advanced hex mesh topologies, followed by the introduction of a novel hex mesh traversal algorithm that navigates hex data structures with up to 58 tets per hex, enabling efficient operation on a wide range of hex meshes. To accompany this algorithm, we propose a set of generic queries that can be used to analyze and visualize hex mesh geometries, demonstrating their potential through a range of example applications. Our proposed algorithm and queries are designed to be versatile and adaptable to various applications, allowing them to be easily integrated into existing toolboxes and customized for specific needs. Through rigorous testing, we validate the performance of our algorithm and demonstrate its robustness across a diverse set of 100 hex meshes, encompassing over 100 million cells and 50 distinct topologies. Our results indicate that the algorithm achieves an average traversal rate of 1.8 billion tets/hour, with a maximum memory requirement of 0.2 GB for the majority of meshes, underscoring its exceptional efficiency and scalability. To facilitate widespread adoption, we publicly release the source code for our algorithm and accompanying queries, along with a comprehensive online benchmarking platform that enables users to test our algorithm on a diverse range of hex meshes. Our platform provides a valuable resource for the scientific community, empowering developers to benchmark their own algorithms against our approach and foster collaborative innovation in hex mesh research. To integrate the link prediction feature into the relation extraction process, we propose two strategies: one involves training a dual-task model for both relation extraction and link prediction, and another involves combining the predicted entity embeddings from the link prediction task with traditional relation extraction methods. Our experimental findings on four datasets reveal that our proposed methods surpass state-of-the-art models in relation extraction and also enhance the performance of link prediction. In reinforcement learning, using continuous state spaces can be complex and
require significant adjustments to the environment or algorithms to become
discrete. Our research focuses on reinforcement learning in metric spaces without
the necessity for state discretization, an approach that is particularly useful
for tasks in virtual environments or with high-dimensional observations. We
develop a novel method that employs a network with a continuous output layer
to determine the next action in a sequence within a trajectory. This action is
used to update the current state in the trajectory, and the reward is calculated.
We prove that our method can find a solution that has zero average reward loss,
and we provide guidance on creating suitable objectives. Additionally, we
demonstrate that our method can learn a continuity constraint, enabling us to
sample from the learned distribution and navigate through the metric space.
Finally, we apply our method to various tasks, including moving a virtual
car to a target location and generating new paths in a video game. Our results
show that our method can learn a distribution that mirrors the data collected
manually. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/alexanderstrathmann/CoarseGrainedContinuity.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning settings, agents are expected to interact with each other in a collaborative environment. However, the traditional approach of independent training by each agent through independent policy updates often leads to unstable and underwhelming results. To address this issue, our proposed transfer empowerment method introduces a social intrinsic motivation that enables agents to recognize and respond to each other's actions in a predictable manner. This is achieved by designing a cooperative learning framework that induces synergistic effects between agents through shared action-observation spaces. By establishing a predictive mechanism for others' behaviors, each agent's policy is motivated to adapt and conform to the expected actions of its counterparts, thereby facilitating effective communication and achieving challenging objectives. Experimental evaluations on various cooperative learning tasks have demonstrated the proposed approach to be highly effective and robust in various cooperative learning tasks. Notably, our method outperformed state-of-the-art benchmarks in cooperative navigation and graph coloring tasks. Furthermore, the underlying mechanism of transfer empowerment was found to be universally applicable and improved communication among agents in multiple existing cooperative learning tasks. Through ablation studies, we found that the proposed method consistently delivered stable and robust performance in diverse cooperative learning tasks. Notably, our method's performance remained consistent even after introducing significant variations in observation and action spaces, as well as intentionally introducing random noise to disrupt agent understanding of each other's behaviors. Overall, our method's ability to induce a social intrinsic motivation that drives predictable behavior among collaborative agents has significant theoretical and practical implications for the design of robust and efficient multi-agent reinforcement learning systems. Object matching is a crucial component of numerous computer vision applications, including 3D reconstruction and tracking. The primary goal of object matching involves identifying corresponding points between two images, specifically key points that share the same semantic meaning. The prevailing method for achieving this, based on descriptors, relies on local descriptors being similar in spatial proximity to determine matching points. However, this approach often fails to account for descriptor variations resulting from factors such as illumination and motion. In contrast, the novel LoFTR method introduced here eschews detectors altogether, instead employing a transformer-based self-attention mechanism to directly establish correspondences through spatially consistent context. The proposed approach demonstrates superior performance in a range of challenging scenarios, including those involving significant variations in lighting and motion. Notably, LoFTR surpasses state-of-the-art performance in the FLIR Benches and the KITTI datasets while boasting a significant speed advantage, executing at a rate of 20 frames per second for high-resolution inputs. The accompanying code has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. Furthermore, the resulting method has been successfully applied to 3D reconstruction in the real-world context of self-driving car video sequences. In this study, we investigate whether it is feasible to obtain a compact and accurate model of a complex system when all that is accessible is a limited representation of its components and interactions. Focusing on Markov Decision Processes as a key challenge, we establish that our task is both necessary and unavoidable in many instances. To address this task, we establish a link between partial observability in Markov Decision Processes and the capacity of the system to learn its own transition function. Building upon this understanding, we propose a novel learning algorithm for Markov Decision Processes with partial observations, and we demonstrate its effectiveness using real-world data from a robotics experiment. Additionally, we explore the applicability of our findings to other fundamental problems in machine learning, including clustering and imitation learning. To facilitate the application of our results, we propose a new representation of partial observations as a compact and structured format, and we discuss its potential uses in the context of Markov Decision Processes. Overall, our research provides a theoretical foundation for our task and highlights its practical implications in machine learning. This study investigates the solutions to elliptic boundary value problems that involve measuring surfaces. Specifically, we consider a measure μ supported on a hypersurface Σ within Ω, a domain in ℝⁿ, and examine the problem -Δu=μ in Ω, with u bounded at its infinity and u(x) approaching 0 as x approaches Σ from within Ω's boundaries. Under certain conditions on μ and Ω, we demonstrate that a continuous function u exists that satisfies these conditions. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between its zero set and Σ, as well as its regularity. This research further generalizes to a broader class of elliptic operators, including those that appear in the study of free boundary problems and singular perturbations. It also has practical implications in the fields of geometry and topology, particularly concerning the existence and properties of maps that map one hypersurface onto another, a topic known as Gelfand problems. In this context, we derive new results regarding the existence and regularity of maps that map Σ onto a target space, while also addressing the existence of the Lagrangian mean curvature of Σ when it is a Lagrangian hypersurface. Lastly, we examine the connection between the properties of these maps and those of the zero set of u. This research was inspired by the findings of Delanois and the second author regarding the existence of non-trivial solutions for Gelfand problems when the measure μ is supported on a set that is homeomorphic to a sphere. Conversely, we demonstrate that if the zero set of u does not resemble a sphere, then a homeomorphism between Σ and its zero set does not exist. In addition, we show that the regularity of the zero set of u is closely tied to that of Σ, as well as to the regularity of the hypersurface Σ. This research also reveals connections to the study of Hardy-type operators and their connections to the study of geometry and topology. This research delves into the potential of continuous-phase modulation (CPM) in non-coherent communication systems, focusing on its resilience to phase distortions via the diverse range of its distinct forms, known as CPM types. CPM can be classified into three categories: 2P, 3P, and 4P, each characterized by its respective polynomial based phase, with 2P types being the most susceptible to phase distortions. As a result, most non-coherent CPM based systems employ 4P types such as GMSK, which can tolerate more phase distortions, albeit at the cost of reduced bandwidth efficiency. However, this paper demonstrates that by utilizing a novel differential detection method, even traditional 2P types can offer superior performance and greater delay tolerance. The proposed differential detection approach involves two distinct steps: first, sampling the received signal at specific intervals based on a pre-defined timing offset, and second, calculating the differential value of the received samples' derivative or original signal's samples' convolution in successive blocks. By analyzing the outcomes of various simulation scenarios, it is evident that the suggested differential detection method significantly enhances the performance of 2P types under severe phase distortion conditions, surpassing the performance of both the conventional differential detection method and the 4P types in most cases. Notably, this technique can be seamlessly integrated into existing communication systems without requiring any modifications to their design or functionality. Furthermore, the experimental findings indicate that the optimal timing offset for the suggested differential detection method varies depending on the specific CPM type in question. The proposed approach has been successfully tested across a range of diverse CPM types, including frequency-hop CPM, binary CPM, GMSK, hexagonal CPM, and multi-carrier CPM. The results of this research suggest that the suggested differential detection method can be a reliable and efficient approach for improving the performance of 2P types in non-coherent communication systems. The experimental data also shed light on the potential applications of this technique in areas such as ultra-wideband and spread spectrum communications. Notably, the analysis of the computational complexity of the proposed approach reveals that it can be implemented using a relatively simple design, with a feasible number of design parameters. However, this threshold depends on another parameter, which can be difficult to estimate. In this research, we introduce a groundbreaking technique called Saliency-guided Indexing (SGI), a rapid and efficient method for locating salient objects in videos using the integration of bottom-up and top-down visual analysis. SGI starts by extracting salient frames from videos, then identifies salient regions within those frames, and finally maps them to specific video segments where relevant. SGI's unique fusion of salient object detection and video indexing accommodates dynamic and structured objects, filling a gap in current research which primarily focuses on static or structured content. Evaluations demonstrate that SGI surpasses leading competitors in both salient object detection and video indexing tasks. Moreover, we have developed a dynamic picture indexing dataset consisting of 100 videos featuring dynamic content, along with a user study that confirms its effectiveness and highlights the importance of salient object information in video indexing. This dataset and SGI implementation are available for further exploration. Notably, SGI's efficiency enables processing of high-resolution videos within 30 seconds using a single GPU. As a result, we anticipate SGI to play a significant role in future research in this area. We introduce a Fixed Point Networks (FPN) approach to train artificial agents to anticipate and accurately predict and react to future game scenarios, specifically near-equilibrium states, by leveraging the application of the Shapley Value to determine fair outcomes. FPNs utilize a two-stage process: the first stage generates potential game scenarios, and the second stage employs a fixed point method to identify the equilibrium of a Markov Game. Notably, traditional fixed point operators cannot be used directly, as they require knowledge of the game's dynamics, which is not available in advance. To address this challenge, we propose a novel learning framework, Fixed Point Networks, that trains a neural network to approximate an operator that can sample near-equilibrium states. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FPNs in single-agent learning without reinforcement, as well as in collaborative learning without rewards, through single-agent and multi-agent scenarios. The results show that FPNs achieve superior performance in various tasks, including predicting game outcomes, anticipating moves in chess, and learning cooperative behaviors in multiple tasks. The learned models can also be used to generate fair outcomes according to the Shapley Value, providing a quantifiable measure of the contribution of each agent. Overall, our proposed framework provides a novel solution to the challenge of training artificial agents to anticipate near-equilibrium states of a Markov Game without reinforcement, opening up new possibilities for applications in game theory and beyond. In magnetic resonance imaging, the L-value represents the number of readings taken from a given pixel, with higher L-values indicating more reliable data. Crowdsourced labeling has become a widely used technique for obtaining large datasets of annotated images. However, the reliability of these labels is compromised by the inclusion of unskilled and untrustworthy contributors who may provide contradictory or incorrect labels. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in datasets with a large number of contributors, where the noise from unreliable sources can overshadow the signal produced by skilled annotators. In this study, we investigate how machine learning models can be adapted to accommodate noisy data. Specifically, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks can effectively distinguish between classes even when provided with imperfect training labels. Furthermore, we propose an innovative method of ensemble modeling that leverages the diversity of contributors' labels to produce more accurate outputs. This ensemble model, known as 'Human Softmax,' utilizes entropy-based metrics to quantify the uncertainty of the models and filter out unreliable class probabilities. Experimental results indicate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in dealing with noisy data. Moreover, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between annotation cost and data quality, shedding light on the optimal strategies for crowdsourcing labels. Ultimately, our findings have significant implications for the design of crowdsourcing tasks and annotation workflows. We investigate the asymptotic properties of the multivariate non-stable time series (MNSTS) at a time point, focusing on a single observation from a sequence with i.i.d. heavy-tailed margins that lack stability. Unlike the univariate case, MNSTS presents unique challenges due to its lack of independence and non-stationarity. By considering two key classes of heavy-tailed distributions - the power-law and the gamma distributions - this study generates precise asymptotic results for the extreme tail behavior of MNSTS. For the power-law case, we demonstrate that a specific statistical estimator yields a consistent, strongly convergent result; for the gamma case, we demonstrate a weaker form of convergence known as almost sure convergence. Notably, these findings reveal distinct asymptotic behaviors for MNSTS and univariate heavy-tailed time series at a time point, with MNSTS exhibiting slower convergence rates. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical application of these theoretical results through simulation examples and a real-world case study involving data from the New York City subway system. This research is expected to contribute significantly to the existing literature on heavy-tailed time series, particularly in the areas of MNSTS and univariate heavy-tailed time series at a time point. Additionally, it is anticipated to have a range of future research opportunities. The accompanying code can be accessed at the provided repository. A related paper focusing on the asymptotic behavior of MNSTS at multiple time points has been published at arXiv:2103.09321. Deep Recurrent Neural Networks are highly effective in handling sequential data but face significant training challenges, particularly regarding communication efficiency when employing federated learning techniques. To address this issue, a new method called DP-REC has been developed to support the secure and efficient training of DLRMs on non-private recurrent neural network tasks while maintaining differential privacy. Surprisingly, our research shows that DP-REC can achieve the same level of accuracy as the non-private model, even with a significant reduction in communication costs of up to 50%. DP-REC's efficacy is demonstrated through our experiments on real-world datasets such as language modeling and sentence classification. Notably, using the generalized outer approximation technique, DP-REC is able to provide a privacy guarantee without compromising its model's performance in terms of accuracy or communication costs. Interestingly, our research reveals that the privacy mechanism itself plays a crucial role in determining model accuracy, highlighting the need for further investigations into the interactions between privacy mechanisms and machine learning model training. By combining a Bloom filter and a hash-based self-certifying filter, we present a new filter collection which satisfies this 'no-cost query' property. Our proposed collection has both a time and a space advantage over previously existing solutions. Furthermore, insertion and deletion operations in our proposed collection have a time complexity of O(d) where 'd' represents the number of filters in the collection. By adapting the self-certifying filter to use 'b' hash functions, we achieve an O(b) time complexity for these operations. Consequently, choosing 'b' sufficiently small allows us to achieve a time complexity of O(d) for insertion and deletion operations. This results in our proposed method outperforming previously existing methods with this regard. Our experiments show that a small 'b' (b = 4) is sufficient to meet this requirement in practice. Utilizing a time-dependent effective theory, we derive an analytical expression for the total cross-section of three-body recombination and verify its applicability in scenarios where laser pulses are turned on and off. Ultimately, our research provides a framework for controlling atomic and molecular state transitions via laser pulses in systems featuring fermionic ultracold gases. Such an approach could be utilized to create specific quantum states, like spin-polarized atoms and spinless molecules. Lastly, our study demonstrates that the recombination process is highly sensitive to the laser detuning, with yields dropping by several orders of magnitude as the detuning increases. Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained attention due to their potential in various applications, including their ability to provide a sense of presence and connection to others. As these robots are controlled using a virtual interface, their ability to deliver high-quality interactions is crucial for their usability. In this research, we conducted a study to evaluate the Quality of Experience (QoE) for Telepresence robot control by investigating how users perceive delays and virtual input inaccuracies. We collected responses from 15 participants who tested the system under different conditions of varying levels of delay and feedback error. Our experiment revealed that users are highly sensitive to delays, even at relatively short latencies, and also notice errors in virtual input, again at relatively short distances. Furthermore, we found that users adapt to some degree of error but still complain about significant inaccuracies, and interestingly, a small amount of delay can make the experience feel more interactive. These findings have practical implications for the design of Telepresence robot control interfaces and provide valuable insights for system designers and engineers. Our study also showcases an adapted version of the Moving Target Technique to evaluate QoE in a time-sensitive environment, and the data we collected can be used to develop performance metrics for Telepresence robot control systems. The concept of model transferability in deep learning refers to the ability of a model to perform well on multiple tasks. Two widely accepted models' agreements regarding transferability are the the Task Daughters Model and the Syntactic Similarity Model. These models suggest that similar tasks share common characteristics, either due to shared underlying factors (the Task Daughters Model) or due to similarities in input data patterns (the Syntactic Similarity Model). However, these models have limitations as they fail to explain the impact of domain differences and the role of input data variability in related tasks. Our study reveals that these models are often invalid as they are based on flawed assumptions. For instance, we show that Task Daughters do not always perform better than unrelated tasks and that domain differences do not always lead to performance variations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Syntactic Similarity Model is also invalid. Our findings indicate that the performance of models on related tasks is largely influenced by noise in the training data. The number of people affected by Alzheimer's disease globally is estimated to be around 50 million and expected to rise to 152 million by 2050. Although there is currently no cure for Alzheimer's, an early diagnosis can help patients live a longer, more comfortable life. However, accurately diagnosing the disease at its early stages is a significant challenge due to the overlap between symptoms of other conditions and those of Alzheimer's. Swarm robotics research has been expanding to incorporate human-swarm interactions, with a focus on enabling swarms to adapt to users' intentions and commands. Despite significant advancements in automated speech recognition technology over the past decade, particularly in English, there remains a persistent shortage of suitable systems for German and other lesser-spoken languages. The invariant-set hypothesis proposes that certain quantum correlations can't be explained by any hidden-variable model. We've examined a specific version of this idea, the'superdeterministic' invariant set, which suggests certain correlations can only be explained by a unique hidden-variable model. To investigate this, we've developed a framework using random variables to represent superdeterministic relationships, which allows us to identify and represent such relationships precisely. However, our analysis shows that these relationships are essentially equivalent to deterministic ones, using the same mathematical framework. This implies that the superdeterministic invariant set likely doesn't exist, and therefore does not rule out the possibility of explaining quantum nonlocality with a single, unique hidden-variable model. We've also expanded upon our framework to explore the concept of 'potent' superdeterministic relationships, which may help shed light on the invariant-set hypothesis. Potent relationships have a significant property: they allow the simultaneous prediction of two specific outcomes, $A_0$ and $A_1$, given the values of $R$ and $A$. We've demonstrated that these relationships can be represented as a combination of deterministic and probabilistic components, which may have implications for understanding the nature of quantum nonlocality. Our analysis also shows that the Bell Tsirelson theorem, which limits certain probability distributions, doesn't play a central role in understanding potent relationships. We've further developed a measure of 'potency strength' and shown that this value can be bounded by a specific range, which may help to better comprehend the nature of quantum nonlocality. This work provides a framework for investigating quantum correlations and their potential explanations within a hidden-variable model framework. It also offers a new perspective on the nature of superdeterministic relationships and the limits of what can be achieved through hidden-variable models. Finally, our analysis provides a new direction for research into the nature of quantum nonlocality, which may help to shed light on the long-standing problem of its explanation within a hidden-variable model framework. The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has led to a corresponding surge in text-based data generated by users. To process this text-based data efficiently, low-power IoT devices require specialized neural network models that can perform keyphrase extraction tasks while being memory-efficient and fast. Current NLP models, typically trained on powerful servers, are often ineffective when deployed on IoT devices due to their significant resource demands. To address this issue, this paper investigates the potential of low-power IoT devices by applying various neural network models to keyphrase detection tasks and comparing their performance in terms of accuracy, memory usage, and processing speed. We introduce a new benchmark, IoTKEY, consisting of multiple text-based datasets that can be executed on IoT devices, and evaluate the performance of 14 NLP models using it. Our study demonstrates that certain models, such as BERT and Transformer, can achieve high accuracy on IoTKEY while being resource-intensive, whereas simpler models like BiLSTM and FastText can provide a good trade-off between accuracy and resource efficiency. To facilitate future research, we publicly release the IoTKEY benchmark and the experimental code on GitHub. Our findings suggest that NLP models' performance depends on the specific dataset and that there is room for improvement in terms of developing more efficient models that can run on IoT devices. We propose that future research should focus on developing methods to adapt existing models to IoT devices' constraints and on developing new models that are specifically designed to be IoT-friendly, using techniques like knowledge distillation and pruning. We also suggest that the IoT community should prioritize developing standards for NLP model deployment on IoT devices, similar to those for CUDA and cuDNN, to make it easier to deploy and manage neural network models on IoT devices. Finally, we propose that the future of IoT NLP should involve developing new models that are specifically designed to be low-power, fast, and accurate, and that can be trained on IoT devices themselves, enabling a more self-sustaining and efficient pipeline from text data to features. To facilitate this vision, we introduce the concept of Self-Sustaining Neural Networks (SSNNs), a new class of neural networks that are designed to be low-power, fast, and accurate, and that can be trained on IoT devices themselves. We demonstrate the feasibility of SSNNs by adapting the BERT model to the IoTKEY dataset and achieving a high accuracy of 0.8159 while reducing its memory usage by 50% and processing time by 75% through a combination of pruning and knowledge distillation. For mixed-priority embedded real-time systems, a new hypervisor called T-Visor is being developed to manage the execution environment for guest operating systems and their applications. The T-Visor hypervisor leverages hardware virtualization technology to provide guest systems with a virtualized computing environment. As a piece of embedded software, T-Visor's performance is heavily influenced by its internal processing mechanisms. The existing research on hypervisor performance primarily focuses on systems with equal importance levels, neglecting real-time systems requiring mixed-priority handling. This paper introduces a T-Visor design tailored to manage real-time systems with hardware virtualization support. The proposed design incorporates a new scheduling strategy, integrated request handling, and memory management, all optimized for real-time systems. The T-Visor's efficiency in handling context switching, system calls, and memory management is evaluated through simulation-based benchmarks, demonstrating its superiority over the current state-of-the-art in hypervisor performance. The results show that T-Visor's context switching and system call overhead are approximately 1.8 and 1.5 times lower, respectively, than the control group. The analysis of these performance metrics enables the derivation of closed-form expressions for T-Visor's real-time overhead, providing valuable insights for optimizing the design and enabling flexible customization of the T-Visor's features. The introduction of T-Visor's design has the potential to revolutionize the development of mixed-priority embedded real-time systems, offering a more practical and efficient design paradigm. The proposed design is versatile, compatible with a wide range of guest operating systems, and has been successfully integrated with two real-time kernels, verifying its performance benefits. We explore the problem of e-commerce product inspection using panoramic stitching. Differing from conventional stitching pipelines that focus on aligning features like power lines or text, we prioritize assessing the shape and features of a product's surface. Given that commercial goods undergo gravitational shaping, we propose using gravity as a prior in our stitching pipeline to expedite the process. A key challenge lies in generating panoramic images while considering the high likelihood of encountering repetitive patterns rather than distinct features. To address this, we introduce a novel method combining minimal answer principles, allowing us to produce a narrow band of potential seams with low entropy, thereby significantly reducing search space from O(n^2) to O(n). Furthermore, we present a simple yet effective approach to generate panoramic images while maintaining high precision. Our approach demonstrates competitiveness and versatility, as it can be applied to various applications, such as monitoring product deformations or detecting defects. Comprehensive evaluations using both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in efficiently generating high-quality panoramic images. Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 95% accuracy in covering 90% of the target area. Automated system repair through controller modification is a complex task, often hindered by the high cost of finding model-based policy errors causing system failures. This paper proposes an approach that leverages probabilistic models to estimate failure rates and apply policy search to develop robust controllers. By representing model uncertainties through probabilistic models, the controller design can be framed as a risk-averse optimization problem, minimizing the likelihood of encountering model-based policy errors during operation. This risk-averse optimization problem can be solved using a robust controller synthesis method, and we evaluate the effectiveness of our approach using a range of probabilistic models, including Gaussian processes and mixture of experts, on a quadrotor flight controller. Our results demonstrate that our approach can achieve a significant reduction in controller failures and outperform traditional policy search methods in the presence of model uncertainties. Additionally, the probabilistic models used in our approach enable us to quantify the uncertainty in the failure rate, allowing us to assess the reliability of the controller and identify the most critical model properties that require further verification. This reliability assessment can be utilized to develop a failure-aware safety controller, capable of detecting and preventing system failures. Our failure-aware safety controller is shown to achieve a zero failure rate and maintain a high level of control performance, while also being applicable to a broader range of control tasks and domains. Overall, the approach proposed in this paper addresses the challenge of automated system repair through controller design, and the failure-aware safety controller developed in this paper can be used to ensure the reliability of control systems in a variety of applications. In the realm of decision-making, the ability to sample, assess, and evaluate experiences effectively has been proven crucial for success. This capability encompasses not just the speed of perception, but also the accuracy and relevance of those experiences. We introduce the concept of "Executive Ability" as a measure of this skill, focusing on the importance of relabeling and resampling perceptions through a review of past events. This review process enables the identification of valuable insights from unproductive efforts and refines existing knowledge to maximize future gains. We propose an efficient algorithm based on contrastive learning to simulate and improve this skill through a game environment, and test its application in the context of playing video games. Our findings suggest that animals may possess "Executive Ability" as a fundamental characteristic, and that its development can be fostered through a structured training program. We also discuss the broader implications of this concept and its potential applications in various fields. This research aims to shed light on the underlying mechanisms of "Executive Ability" and its role in decision-making, and we anticipate that these findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of this skill in both humans and animals. Event detection has been extensively researched, yet the related event extraction remains under-explored, primarily due to the scarcity of quality datasets that align with real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce Multilingual Event Extraction, a groundbreaking dataset containing detailed information about real-world events observed in multiple languages. The dataset comprises two parts: (1) discerning whether an event occurs in a given mention, and (2) identifying key aspects associated with that event if it occurs. The dataset spans 10 topics, 5 languages, and covers over 20 million mentions, with nearly 70% of them serving as positive instances for the first task and approximately 30% qualifying for the second. Given its massive scale, the dataset presents significant challenges, including an overall accuracy of 83.35% for task one and 54.93% for task two, with performance disparities ranging from 10 to 30% across various language groups. To facilitate further research, we present a baseline model that leverages pre-trained language models, achieving an accuracy of 83.05% for task one and 53.92% for task two. Recent advancements in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have led to remarkable performance in various tasks, yet their instability and lack of explainability remain significant hurdles. To address the first issue, researchers have effectively applied techniques like stability metrics and loss-based methods to enhance GAN training. However, their lack of interpretability makes it difficult to understand the generated content. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes hidden space explanations to provide context for GAN-generated material, with a particular focus on image data. Our proposed method, HS2DISC, incorporates an additional hidden space layer in the discriminator, allowing it to pinpoint specific semantic regions in generated images. Through backpropagation, HS2DISC estimates the impact of real image features on these identified regions, effectively mapping regional explanations to specific images. To achieve explainability, HS2DISC employs an iterative optimization process that inverts this mapping to produce explainatory codes, which are then combined with a generator-produced image to create an explainable output. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that HS2DISC significantly enhances the stability and interpretability of multiple state-of-the-art GAN architectures, with impressive results in image generation, localization, and explainability tasks. Our findings indicate that improved GAN training using metrics like Frechet Inception Distance (FID) and Interpretable FID (IFID) can be achieved by integrating HS2DISC. Moreover, human evaluations confirm that HS2DISC surpasses other explainability methods in terms of semantic accuracy and overall quality. Our implementation of HS2DISC is available at https://github.com/Deep-Local/HS2DISC. With HS2DISC, we aim to significantly advance the state-of-the-art in GAN training metrics and image explainability. Our work also sets a new standard for evaluating GANs based on their interpretability, with the proposed IFID score serving as a benchmark for measuring both stability and interpretability in a unified manner. Our research is further distinguished by its focus on developing a general method for image explainability that can be applied to multiple GAN architectures, with the potential to enhance explainability in other computer vision tasks as well. Our work is also complementary to existing research on training more stable GANs, with the proposed HS2DISC method addressing the previously underemphasized aspect of interpretability. A novel computational strategy has been developed to efficiently model and forecast the complex interactions between wind turbines and harsh marine environments, specifically for their structural loading during turbulent storms. This innovative approach combines two Gaussian Process regression methods in a sequence, utilizing a standard Gaussian Process model for the initial prediction and incorporating an adaptive, Gaussian Process-based model for subsequent predictions, which utilizes historical data from the first model. This adaptive strategy adjusts the Gaussian Process model's input parameters to optimize its predictions. When evaluating this strategy against a traditional two-stage Gaussian Process model, which employs an emulator model for preliminary predictions and an adaptive GP model for subsequent predictions, the results demonstrate significantly reduced computational costs for high-resolution predictions, a 70% decrease in total computational time. Additionally, the proposed strategy's predictions show minimal discrepancies with the results from high-resolution dynamic simulations, averaging less than 2% error for specific load types, revealing strong correlations between wind turbine structural loads and environmental factors, and identifying key environmental risk factors, including hub-height wind speed, wave height, and turbulent wind fluctuations. Optimization algorithms rely heavily on second derivative information, captured by the Hessian matrix's generalized structure. While the innermost part is efficiently computable, optimizing algorithms often struggle with the outer layer, forcing a compromise between computational cost and accuracy. This paper introduces a new, ViViT model, which approximates the outer Hessian layer with ease, by reinterpreting the generalized Gauss-Newton's inner and outer layers through its diminished structure. This promises improved performance and faster convergence for numerical optimization algorithms. ViViT's potential is further explored in deep learning's diagonal and vertical regulation frameworks. Our experiments show that ViViT's accuracy far surpasses computational cost in various settings, making it a valuable tool across machine learning disciplines. This research also sheds light on the generalized Gauss-Newton's diminished structure, paving the way for future research. This paper explores the concept of interdependent networks of networks as a model for understanding how systems with strong dependencies fail during major disruptions. We introduce an integrated management system that shares information across all interconnected networks, fostering cooperation and mutual assistance in times of crisis. To test the efficacy of this approach, we analyze a scenario involving networks of networks failing in rapid succession and investigate a case study based on the United States power grid, finding that its networks tend to fail in a chain reaction. In contrast, our proposed management system is shown through simulations to be highly effective in preventing such failures, suggesting the importance of developing intelligent networks that work together to enhance resilience. Our research also raises questions about the optimal level of integration in networks, suggesting that highly interconnected systems may not always be more resilient than those with weaker ties.
