Blazars are known for emitting strong, variable X-ray and gamma-ray spectra, 
originating from jets within their nuclei. In these jets, electrons can collide 
with the surrounding photon bath, causing a surplus of low-energy photons via 
the External Compton scattering process. This scattering can occur in two distinct 
ways, either with a randomly polarized photon field resulting in unpolarized 
scattered light or with a highly aligned and partially polarized photon field, 
yielding polarized and potentially variable scattered light. This study explores 
the latter, inverse polarized scattering, as a possible explanation for the UV and 
soft X-ray excess often seen in blazar spectra. This excess is typically attributed to 
emission from the blazar's jet, but the nature of this emission remains uncertain. 
Using a Monte Carlo simulation, the MAPPIES model has been developed to analyze 
this phenomenon and its potential application to the Mkn 421 spectrum is 
investigated. This model has been further refined to account for the effects of 
magnetic fields on the photon fields, as well as the variable, time-dependent 
magnetic field in the blazar's region. This time-dependent field is thought to be 
responsible for the observed variability in blazar spectra, and its inclusion in the 
model has been shown to improve the alignment of the model and observational data. 
Using this model, the authors are able to replicate the observed Mkn 421 spectrum 
and variability, and infer the presence of a power law distribution of electron 
energies. This study provides a framework for understanding the nature of the 
emission from the blazar's jet and its potential application to the observed 
spectra. The authors also discuss the potential limitations of this model and its 
application to other blazars, as well as its potential implications for the

A decentralized learning technique called Federated Learning utilizes a centralized server to process machine-owned models through several iterations of model updating and aggregation. Research has shown that FL's aggregated model formation process may unintentionally create discriminatory results when trained on biased data. Moreover, the traditional FL method fails to account for data privacy, leading to potential equity concerns despite the aggregated nature. To address these issues, we first analyze the potential for equity in FL's model updates and propose alternative methods, including a new bias-aware FL protocol. Subsequently, we investigate how incorporating differential privacy can be applied to FL and introduce a new framework, Federated Learning with Local Differential Privacy (FLLDP), which ensures privacy at the individual machine level. Our experiments demonstrate that privacy-enhancing FL can still achieve high predictive performance. Notably, our findings suggest that privacy has a more substantial impact on accuracy than bias, highlighting the need to balance these factors in FL's design. Lastly, we outline potential directions for further research in the areas of bias and privacy in FL. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zyk420/baselfed. We developed an alternative approach to quantum key distribution, leveraging
the properties of dual-field states, and have successfully demonstrated its
improved efficiency and versatility. This scheme's ability to operate without
requiring phase stabilization between the two communicating parties greatly
reduces the complexity of our method. Instead, we utilize the established
method of cross-correlation measurement to generate a secret key. Our
experimental results, using phase-shift keying signals, have yielded a key
generation rate of 1.73 Mkeys per second at a low error threshold of 1.87%,
and we have also tested the scheme's robustness by verifying it can operate
effectively despite significant phase differences between the two parties. 
Furthermore, our method's ability to handle arbitrary input states makes it
suitable for working with high-order dual-field states generated through
coherent amplitude-shift keying, enabling the potential for high-speed QKD
applications over long distances via fiber. This research has led to a deeper
understanding of dual-field QKD and has paved the way for the development of
next-generation, high-speed QKD systems. Our method's simplicity and
efficiency make it an attractive option for building secure communication
systems in the future. Our experimental results are presented in a format
suitable for publication.

Object detection techniques have been used to identify specific objects within images, but the current approaches are limited by the requirement for detailed object information, including class labels and spatial data, which are not readily available for all situations. To overcome this limitation, large-scale detection tasks often rely on smaller, closed datasets with complete annotations, before merging them into a larger combined dataset. However, this method has its limitations as it can only accommodate certain types of objects, severely limiting the scope of what can be learned. In this research, we explore the use of pseudo labels to facilitate open-set object detection, a task that involves identifying unknown objects, without prior knowledge of their class labels or spatial distribution. To achieve this, we have developed a multi-stage framework that combines image and text information to generate pseudo labels, before refining them through a specialized re-detection process. Experimental results from three benchmark datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods, with improvements of up to 8.5% in detection accuracy for certain tasks. Recent breakthroughs in neural architecture search (NAS) have been impressive, 
but many NAS approaches have been hindered by the problem of transfer 
disadvantages - when a model is trained and tested on different data sets, 
performance often drops significantly. In this paper, we first show that 
transfer disadvantages in NAS are primarily caused by the interference issue, 
where different architecture components and their co-occurring combinations store 
information in the model simultaneously. We then investigate the impact of 
interference on NAS by introducing a simple yet effective metric called 
co-occurrence frequency and demonstrate its significant influence on the model's 
performance. Finally, we design a novel architecture search algorithm called 
Interference Minimization Search (IMS) that intentionally minimizes the 
interference by avoiding the selection of architectures with high co-occurrence 
frequencies, thus leading to better generalization and overall performance. Our 
experiments show that IMS outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods by a 
substantial margin, with a notable improvement of up to 2.4% in top-1 accuracy 
on CIFAR-10 and 8.4% on ImageNet. Moreover, IMS achieves this achievement without 
any additional modifications to the model, thus saving significant computational 
resources. Our code is available at https://github.com/whwu/IMS. IMS has the 
potential to address the transfer disadvantages in NAS and achieve better 
generalization, thus opening up new possibilities for future research in this 
area. Moreover, IMS can be easily integrated into existing NAS methods to 
significantly enhance their performance, thus offering a practical solution to 
improve the current state-of-the-art methods. Our research provides new 
insights into the transfer disadvantages in NAS and offers a new perspective on

robust and efficient NAS methods that can handle the transfer disadvantages and 
achieve better generalization. Our research is available at

As such, it can produce biased results for data sets like directional data, virtual metastates, and high-dimensional data with restricted ranges. To address this issue, we propose an alternative to t-SNE, referred to as vmf-SNE, tailored for data that lies within a sphere and adheres to the von Mises-Fisher distribution. In real-world rail networks, multiple simultaneous timetables often need to be optimized concurrently, which can make it challenging to efficiently allocate processing resources among these individual timetables. To address this issue, we propose the Multitasking Timetabling Problem (MTP), a generic optimization problem that encompasses various timetabling applications as specialized instances. The MTP involves dividing available computing resources among a set of processing tasks, each corresponding to a specific timetabling problem, with the goal of minimizing total processing costs while maximizing the solution quality within time limits for each task. To solve MTP, we suggest a range of heuristics, starting with a basic one that distributes processing time equally among tasks, and followed by more advanced methods that sequential assign tasks, as well as a local search heuristic that reassigns tasks to improve solution quality. The effectiveness of our proposed heuristics is demonstrated through experiments on the Timetable Construction Problem (TBP), where we show that by concurrently processing instances of TBP using MTP, we can achieve better results than optimizing each instance individually. Furthermore, we also investigate how MTP can be applied to other real-world timetabling problems, such as the School Timetable Problem (STP) and the University Course Timetable Problem (UCTP), and present initial findings. The MTP formulation and accompanying heuristics are implemented in a Java-based open-source software package, which is available for direct use or as a starting point for further development. The proposed heuristics have been validated using a comprehensive dataset comprising 60 TBP instances, 20 STP instances, and 20 UCTP instances, and our results show that our methods can tackle these problems more effectively than existing specialized algorithms. The analysis of our experimental outcomes highlights the importance of further investigation into the MTP problem, which has the potential to significantly contribute to the advancement of both the MTP field and the broader Multitasking Optimization (MO) domain. The study also sheds light on the current limitations of MO research and identifies promising avenues for future exploration. A widely used and formal framework for temporal planning is TPTL, which has a well-defined semantics in a multi-layered structure, separating the syntax from the semantics to ensure the correctness of its definitions. This work builds on previous studies by integrating TPTL with standard planning technology to assess plan quality, and in turn, enhances the accuracy of TPTL by rectifying errors found in its initial implementation. By decoupling the syntax from the semantics in TPTL, and separating the roles of a syntax module for formal representation and a runtime module for practical execution, the ambiguity in TPTL's semantics is resolved. Specifically, a semantics mismatch was discovered in TPTL's implementation, causing an unsound outcome in plan validation. This work addresses the issue and confirms the soundness of TPTL's validation by revising the semantics to align with its intended definition. Moreover, a practical validation algorithm is developed to determine whether a given state satisfies a plan's conditions. The integration of TPTL with standard planning technology utilises the planning as language (PVL) interface to translate TPTL planning problems into planning domains and instances, and uses a standard planner to produce high-quality plans. However, due to an implementation error in TPTL's time function, the planner produces plans that are semantically flawed. This work addresses the issue and rectifies the error in TPTL's implementation, and confirms the correctness of its time function. The integration of TPTL with standard planning technology is then re-attempted, and the resulting plans are validated using the developed algorithm to ensure their correctness. Finally, the work demonstrates the effectiveness of TPTL's validation by comparing its results with those of a sound but informally defined validation method in the planning community. The results show that TPTL's validation is sound and produces semantically correct plans, and that its validation aligns with the informal validation method but provides more accurate outcomes. In summary, the work enhances the accuracy of TPTL's validation by revising its implementation to align with its intended definition, and by developing a formal semantics and validation algorithm to ensure the correctness of its time function and plan validation. The work also integrates TPTL with standard planning technology and confirms the correctness of its time function and plan validation. The large-scale integration of decentralized energy sources such as batteries and flexible electrical loads presents challenges for optimizing infrastructure development. In particular, the placement of these resources can greatly affect the optimal design of new power networks, yet current decision support systems often treat their spatial distribution as random and uncontrollable. As a result, the networks designed using these systems tend to be over-expanded, leading to increased costs for investors. In this paper, we investigate the responsiveness of power network expansion models to the characteristics and locations of distributed resources. We achieve this by developing a novel optimization model for extending power networks to minimize costs, and then integrating it with a generator's investment decisions in a sequential framework. The results of our case studies indicate that networks designed using traditional methods are indeed overly expensive due to their lack of consideration for the variables influencing resource deployment. Furthermore, our research reveals that the characteristics of resources can be categorized into two distinct types: those that reduce load during network planning and increase demand during network operation, and those that are unresponsive to their spatial deployment. In contrast to the second type, the first presents opportunities for the generator to manipulate resource deployment and thereby influence the optimal network design. Consequently, the generator can exploit this flexibility to adjust the timing of resource commissioning and influence the load during network operation to minimize costs, while also adjusting the timing of resource decommissioning to minimize losses. Our results demonstrate that the optimal timing of resource commissioning varies based on the characteristics of resources, and highlight the need for the generator to balance the load during network operation to minimize losses. Moreover, the results show that the optimal timing of resource decommissioning depends on the characteristics of resources, and that the deployment of resources with variable output can enhance network resilience. This study examines the global electrodynamics of a single species of ions in a contained area with smooth boundaries, addressing the Confined Vlasov-Poisson system. In contrast to traditional Vlasov-Poisson models, we explore the scenario where the confining walls are perfectly conducting, impermeable, and subject to a constant electric field. We demonstrate the existence of solutions to this system under minimal assumptions on the initial conditions and show that these solutions remain unique for all time. Furthermore, we expand our analysis to a broader class of models, including the Confined Vlasov-Poisson-Maxwell system, under similar conditions to establish analogous results. Our work builds upon and generalizes existing solutions to these systems, particularly for the single species Confined Vlasov-Poisson and Maxwell-VD systems. Moreover, we successfully apply our analysis to obtain global existence and uniqueness results for coupled electron-ion plasmas in a confined environment. In doing so, we address a long-standing open question in the field. All solutions to these systems are classically smooth, albeit the electron component may exhibit a singularity in certain scenarios. This research represents an extension of prior works on non-confined and perfectly conducting domains to confined domains with Neumann boundary conditions, as well as a generalization to a broader class of models, under minimal and maximally dissipative assumptions. We have successfully applied and expanded the techniques developed in a companion paper, initially designed for the single species Confined Vlasov-Poisson system, to a variety of models, while addressing the non-trivial case of coupled electron-ion plasmas for the first time. We have also established the existence of smooth solutions for the Confined Vlasov-Poisson system in a perfectly conducting domain, a result previously unknown in the literature. In doing so, we have successfully overcome the limitations imposed by the non-smooth electric potential, as well as the non-trivial case of coupled electron-ion plasmas, requiring the use of De Laval nozzle initial data. We have also explored the scenario of coupled electron-ion plasmas in a confined domain with perfectly conducting walls, under quasineutral conditions, demonstrating the existence of smooth solutions for a long time. This research represents an extension of prior works on the single species and coupled electron-ion plasmas to a confined domain with perfectly conducting walls, under various assumptions. We have also successfully applied the techniques developed in a companion paper to a broader class of models, under minimal and maximally dissipative assumptions.

The Collatz Conjecture remains an unsolved problem in the field of number theory, describing a sequence of numbers where any given starting point is subjected to a series of transformations: if the number is even, it's divided by two, if it's odd, it's replaced by the product of itself and three, then one, before eventually reaching a repeating pattern of the number sequence. This phenomenon is known as the Collatz sequence, and a key assertion is that no matter what starting point is chosen, the sequence will always converge to a repeating pattern of the number sequence. This prediction has been extensively tested and verified for nearly every starting point, with the exception of a small subset consisting of numbers that are not of the form $4k$ for some integer $k$. This unverified claim has garnered significant interest and debate among mathematicians, with many experts believing it to be true. While some have developed mathematical arguments in its favor, others have created counterarguments. Despite extensive research, a definitive proof of the Collatz Conjecture has yet to be found. As a result, mathematicians have dubbed it one of the most enduring and intriguing unsolved problems in mathematics. The primary goal of 3D fusion from LiDAR and cameras involves merging geometric and photometric data to create a rich 3D scene. Historically, camera-based fusion techniques have excelled due to their ability to provide color information crucial for distinguishing LiDAR-derived points. Conversely, direct approaches often fall short due to color noise, leading to inconsistent 3D reconstructions. To address this challenge, researchers have developed multi-modal fusion techniques, but many rely on complex and brittle features. To overcome these limitations, we introduce BEVFusion, a novel and versatile framework that combines bird's-eye-view features from both sensors. Specifically, it fuses LiDAR data with combined bird's-eye-view image and feature map from the camera, then projects the results back to the original sensor coordinates. This approach allows for the effective incorporation of color information while utilizing LiDAR data for more accurate 3D reconstructions. Our method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI dataset, outperforming other fusion techniques. Moreover, it achieves real-world success on various 3D applications, including autonomous driving and robotics. Notably, it has been successfully deployed in the self-driving technology platform Autopilot by Tesla. Our code is available for public access at https://github.com/TeslaSense/BEVFusion. The phenomenon of laser-induced self-modulation in liquids has garnered significant attention due to its capacity to produce intricate diffraction patterns. These patterns result from the combined effects of laser interaction with the liquid's inherent refraction, absorption, and scattering characteristics. In our investigation, we rigorously examined the temporal and spatial thermal response of the liquid, taking into account varying laser parameters, absorption depths, and thermal diffusivities. Our findings reveal that the formation of complex self-induced diffraction patterns is contingent upon precise synchronization of thermal wave arrival times at the detector and depth-dependent phase matching. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough comprehension of laser-induced self-modulation in liquids. Additionally, we propose a novel method for measuring liquid scattering coefficients via angular-dependent measurements of laser-induced self-modulation. This approach offers an alternative to conventional methods like spectrophotometry and dynamic light scattering. Experimental validation of our proposed technique is also presented. Ultimately, our investigation provides a comprehensive analytical framework for interpreting and predicting the intricate self-induced diffraction patterns observed in liquids. This framework is expected to facilitate novel applications in liquid-based diffractive optics and light manipulation. A supporting software package, available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7540408, enables users to input specific experimental parameters and simulate the resulting self-induced diffraction patterns observed in liquids. A supplementary video showcasing the simulated diffraction patterns is available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m1.eoahak9m5y.aj.

This pipeline integrates stream processing operators with data history querying capabilities, supported by a unified distributed computing platform. The H-STREAM architecture, comprising a stream processing layer and a data storage layer, enables both temporary data processing and permanent data analysis with integrated analytics services. The pipeline's components, including parallel data processing and a distributed index for data storage, ensure scalability and efficiency, as demonstrated through an example use case of interactive data exploration. The H-STREAM architecture, as part of a larger framework called Hadoop Massively Parallel Ad-Hoc Data Analysis (HMAPA), facilitates the creation of various analytics pipelines with unique features. These pipelines can be leveraged to address specific challenges in real-time analytics applications, as exemplified by HMAPA. The architecture's design allows for seamless integration of new features and modules, as well as efficient data management through a stream processing layer. Recent research has shown promising results for using deep learning to translate SPARQL queries and natural language descriptions through models such as SPARQL-NMT. However, SPARQL-NMT models struggle to maintain accuracy when dealing with queries containing complex and lengthy component combinations. To address this limitation, we introduce a new approach that utilizes a duplicate mechanism for managing SPARQL-KB component representations in the SPARQL-NMT framework. This duplicate mechanism enables each component to be treated as an individual, thereby allowing SPARQL-NMT to learn from its experiences and improve its translations. Furthermore, we propose a new attention mechanism for SPARQL-NMT, specifically designed to facilitate the exchange of information between SPARQL component representations. Experimental evaluations of our proposed approach on various benchmark datasets demonstrate significant improvements in performance, with average MRR scores increasing by 2.17, 1.88, and 1.45 for DBpedia, YAGO2, and NIST-GOLD datasets respectively. The associated code and model implementations can be accessed at the provided repository link. The resulting models achieved top-3 rankings in the NIST SPARQL Challenge 2021. The increasing use of neural networks in control systems has led to a pressing need to establish a systematic approach for validating their reliability. This study aims to introduce a framework for verifying the properties of neural networks used in control applications, building on prior research in validating control systems with polynomial behaviors. To address the challenges posed by neural networks' non-linear and data-driven nature, this framework is tailored to accommodate the unique characteristics of these models. Specifically, this study assumes access to a trained neural network, a mathematical representation of its input-output behavior through an implicit equation, and an ability to adjust its parameters via gradient-based optimization. To demonstrate the framework's applicability, this research proposes a method for validating neural networks in control systems through a series of iterative procedures, ultimately enabling the verification of reachability and control synthesis specifications. This approach is substantiated by various numerical examples, including high-dimensional systems, demonstrating its potential for analyzing complex scenarios. Moreover, this study showcases the framework's capabilities on two real-world applications: (1) a self-driving vehicle navigating around obstacles and (2) a quadrotor aircraft performing a trajectory-tracking task. To facilitate the adoption of neural networks in control systems, this research provides a toolbox with open-source code and offers practical guidance on their development and deployment. Ultimately, this study aims to bridge the gap between the widespread adoption of neural networks in control applications and their rigorous mathematical validation. Clustering methods are extensively employed in numerous scientific disciplines to derive insights from complex data sets. Researchers have developed clustering algorithms that can handle dependencies between multiple variables, using matrix decompositions such as PCA, ICA, and non-negative matrix factorization. However, these methods do not account for relationships between groups of variables during the grouping process. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a functorial framework to construct a hierarchical tree of groups of variables. Our method enables the grouping of sets of sets of variables, allowing for overlap between groups and making it applicable to data sets with diverse structures. The algorithm's output can be represented as a category theory concept called a directed complex, providing a comprehensive organizational structure for the data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to identify non-obvious, highly nested groups of variables. Real-world data streams often compromise the integrity of received data, necessitating reliable restoration. To achieve this, a method based on tensor ring decomposition has been developed for streaming data repair. This approach employs a novel, patch-monitoring guided framework to tackle the limitations of tensor ring, including incomplete and wrapped data streaming. By integrating monitoring with adaptive window adjustment and tensor ring decomposition, a linear restoration process is ensured, even in the face of unpredictable data wrapping. This framework also accommodates diverse data types and repair scenarios. Our method's efficacy has been validated through multiple experiments, demonstrating superior restoration quality and superior performance compared to traditional methods. Notably, our method achieves a 10-fold improvement in restoration speed. This technique has been successfully applied to visual data recovery, including the repair of distorted images and compressed video decoding. In a recent experiment, researchers observed that the spectrum of inertial wave turbulence in rotating disks follows the Kolmogorov spectrum $E(f) \sim f^{-7/3}$. To further understand this phenomenon, we conducted computational studies to investigate the energy spectrum of inertial wave turbulence using both Hamiltonian and forced approaches. The results showed that the energy spectrum follows $E(f) \sim f^{-7/3}$ in both scenarios, confirming that this spectrum is a universal property of inertial wave turbulence. Notably, we found that the spectrum $E(f) \sim f^{-7/3}$ persists even when the energy transfer is not localized around a characteristic frequency. Additionally, we observed that the spectrum is independent of the disk's geometric characteristics, such as the number of grid points in the tangential and normal directions. To validate our model, we also calculated the transverse velocity spectrum using the forward cascade model and obtained $E_{\perp}(f) \sim f^{-7/3}$. Overall, our findings provide strong evidence for the validity of the Kolmogorov spectrum in inertial wave turbulence. This study examines how significantly modified images impact human and machine perception. We contend that intense alterations in images are perceived differently by humans and machines due to varying dependencies on contextual information. In this research, a large number of humans evaluated images with heavily modified context, and the results were compared with the responses of state-of-the-art visual scene understanding models. We also investigate the effect of image degradation on visual scene understanding models and demonstrate that these models are more susceptible to image alterations. Furthermore, we introduce IALM, a dataset consisting of images with intense local modifications, and show that it can be effectively utilized to train visual scene understanding models to be more resilient to such intense alterations. The dataset and models discussed in this research are accessible via https://ialm-dataset.github.io. Our findings are presented at the CVPR 2021 main track. Researchers have created a quantum Monte Carlo program to examine the properties of two-dimensional arrays of three interconnected spin units that interact weakly with one another. The program's focus is on materials called BaCaNiO$_3$ and its derivatives, whose spin units are linked by a unique 'ring exchange' interaction. The results show that in the full lattice, there's no long-range order when there's no external pressure or when it's applied at low temperatures. However, under moderate pressures or at high temperatures, the material exhibits an antiferromagnetic arrangement of spin units in a triangular pattern. The pressure-induced changes to the material's magnetic structure have been explained using a simple model based on the material's cluster magnetism. The research also reveals that under certain conditions, the material's magnetic units are connected by spin units, resulting in a non-universal behavior that deviates from established theories of quantum materials. where the goal is to accurately predict the evolution of relationships within 
dynamic entities over time. A significant challenge in this area is addressing 
the significant data imbalance often present in temporal knowledge graphs, 
where earlier events are more frequently recorded due to limitations in data 
retention. To tackle this issue, researchers have developed methods utilizing 
sliding time windows and graph construction. However, these methods are 
inflexible and fail to leverage early information from later time periods. 
Furthermore, existing research has largely neglected the link forecasting 
application, which involves predicting future relationships in a temporal 
knowledge graph. In this study, we investigate the link forecasting task and 
propose a novel framework, called StaticLink, which utilizes static 
infrastructure to generate hypothetical relationships across the entire time span 
of a temporal knowledge graph. Specifically, we employ a static graph 
construction method to generate relationships at various points in the past, 
aggregate these using attention-based mechanisms, and then apply a scoring 
inference to identify potential links. Notably, our framework addresses the 
issue of data imbalance and is adaptable to accommodate data from any time 
period. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on two real-world 
temporal knowledge graphs and demonstrate its superiority over existing 
benchmark methods. Additionally, we conduct an in-depth analysis of our 
approach and provide recommendations for future research in link forecasting.

The proliferation of edge devices like IoT sensors and mobile devices has led to a surge in distributed machine learning demands. However, the diversity in device capabilities and link connectivity has made traditional machine learning approaches impractical for distributed training. To address this challenge, we propose a novel asynchronous distributed training framework for nonlinear regression on edge devices under varying resource and link conditions. Specifically, we develop a federated gradient descent algorithm that adapts to non-identically and non-stationarily distributed data on each edge device. Furthermore, we propose an adaptive local epoch determination method to optimize device participation in global averaging, taking into account communication limitations and edge device data freshness. In addition, we employ a lightweight communication strategy that transmits device-specific model updates in binary format via quantization. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets and diverse edge device settings demonstrate that our proposed framework surpasses existing approaches in resource efficiency and convergence speed. Notably, under resource-constrained settings, our algorithm achieves a 2.3x speedup and 2.3x efficiency improvement over the state-of-the-art, while maintaining comparable convergence performance. Moreover, our framework's efficiency is found to be inversely correlated with the strength of edge device resources, thereby validating its practicality for resource-scarse edge devices. Overall, our findings suggest that edge devices can collaboratively support complex machine learning tasks, and our proposed framework serves as a crucial stepping stone for future research in distributed machine learning. Building upon this framework, we develop a distributed regulation strategy that maintains stability and performance without relying on a central controller. Furthermore, we prove that the proposed approach achieves comparable performance to a central controller with complete system information, and present a user-friendly design method with analytically derived stability and performance guarantees. Notably, the proposed architecture is versatile and applicable to various system configurations and information exchange scenarios, and can be easily scaled up for large systems with numerous channels and agents. Lastly, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through comprehensive numerical experiments. The presented work has the potential to address the challenges of decentralized control and regulation, and can be widely adopted in real-world applications. To address these concerns, Federated Learning has emerged as a promising solution for developing robust vehicle models without compromising user privacy. Nevertheless, this approach poses new challenges related to user authentication, file verification, and model security, which can be overcome by leveraging Blockchain technology. Motivated by the potential of Blockchain in enhancing FL, this article conducts an in-depth analysis of recent developments in Blockchain-based FL systems, with a particular focus on the Internet of Vehicles. Our comprehensive review encompasses 64 key papers, categorizing them according to their primary contributions and discussing the strengths, weaknesses, and future research directions in this area. Our ultimate goal is to provide a thorough understanding of Blockchain and FL, as well as to pinpoint areas requiring further investigation. Based on our findings, we propose three potential avenues for future research: 1) Developing a comprehensive evaluation framework for Blockchain-based FL systems, 2) Exploring the feasibility of Decentralized Blockchain and Distributed Ledger technologies, and 3) Investigating the application of Blockchain and FL in emerging fields such as Industry 4.0 and 5G. By identifying these research gaps, we hope to inspire future research in this area. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive literature survey table summarizing the key papers in Blockchain and FL, along with relevant indices for further reference. Our work is expected to serve as a valuable resource for researchers, practitioners, and students working in this area. Our approach also accounts for representation's variability and translates into a highly effective supervised classifier for detecting specific epigenetic marks using mock reads from an experimental pipeline. Notably, our method surpasses the performance of supervised competitors, including attention-based models, across various scenarios, particularly in scarce data settings. Furthermore, the representation learned through this method exhibits remarkable transferability to related problems, such as cross-species classification. Implementing this method requires only an off-the-shelf deep learning library and a standard computational environment, making it highly accessible for a wide range of researchers and practitioners. Our solution is available as an open-source contribution to the deepDNA project on GitHub. Through thorough experimentation, our work demonstrates the potential of unsupervised representation learning to address complex problems in computational epigenetics and other fields. The learned representations can be further explored using tools like DeepEye for visualization. Our results also shed light on the characteristics of the representation, revealing that attention mechanisms focus on specific nucleotide sequences and epigenetic marks, and the learned features are highly interpretable. Ultimately, the integration of unsupervised representation learning and attention mechanisms offers a promising direction for future research in computational epigenetics and related areas. The prevalence of hate speech on social media platforms poses a significant threat to users' mental health and safety. Research has revealed a strong correlation between hate speech and increased anxiety, depression, and even suicidal tendencies. To combat this issue, researchers have been working to develop effective hate speech detection models. To address this limitation, we propose a novel characteristic extraction model that captures the essence of hate speech across different categories of offensive content. Our approach involves extracting distinct features of hate speech within a dataset and then training a classifier using these characteristics. Our results show that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving an accuracy of 82.2% on the Hate2019 dataset, which surpasses the current best-performing model's accuracy of 78.7%. Additionally, the extracted characteristics have the potential to shed light on the underlying patterns in hate speech content, which can be utilized to inform the development of social media moderation policies. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of characteristic extraction in hate speech detection and highlight its potential as a versatile approach for natural language processing tasks. Furthermore, the extracted characteristics can be used to create more targeted and effective social media moderation policies, which can in turn contribute to improved mental health and safety outcomes for social media users. Our method's success can be attributed to the distinct features of hate speech content, which our model was able to effectively capture and utilize. A novel statistical model is introduced to analyze data on multiple events occurring over a long period of time. This information is represented through the concept of complex paths in life, specifically focusing on individuals who have experienced a myocardial infarction and examining the progression of cardiovascular disease. A two-part model is proposed to evaluate the probability of multiple events happening at different times, taking into account the connections between these events and incorporating individual features that change over time. A new type of distribution is used to analyze the event occurrences, allowing for event-specific information to be incorporated. Simulation studies assess the model's performance under various data conditions. When applied to the Reversa Myocardium study, the model reveals significant and useful information about the progression of heart disease in people who have experienced a heart attack. This type of analysis can help healthcare providers understand the potential causes and consequences of a heart attack more clearly and develop targeted interventions accordingly. A web-based platform is also created to support the use of this new approach in real-world healthcare settings. This provides a basis for constructing self-dual solutions, known as twistor constructions. Specifically, this approach enables the creation of solutions for Einstein's equations as well as Yang-Mills theory itself. We also utilize the spinor formalism to describe these solutions in spacetime. Furthermore, our results resolve the long-standing problem of formulating an action for self-dual Yang-Mills theory with an anti-self-dual sector. This work draws on the principles of twistor theory, specifically the concept of creating non-linear fields from linear ones, and relies on the advanced mathematical concepts of supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory on twistor space and the spinor representation of conformal algebra. The resulting field theory is invariant under the full conformal group, although this symmetry is expected to be partially broken by quantum effects, in line with the principles of twistor theory. The construction of solutions is facilitated by the use of harmonic twistor spinors, subject to delta constraints that reflect the constraints on the spinor helicity in spacetime. This method is analogous to the approach used in constructing solutions for the self-dual Yang-Mills equations on twistor space, and draws on the principles of harmonic supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory on twistor space. The resulting solutions can be viewed as a specific instance of the broader class of solutions to Einstein's equations as self-dual representatives of the Penrose inequality. Using density functional theory, we investigate the electronic properties of silicene decorated with manganese, situated on a layer of hexagonal boron nitride. Results indicate that manganese takes on a +2 charge and forms a coordinate bond with the nitrogen atoms of the substrate. In comparison to free manganese atoms, our findings show that the adlayer manganese atoms exhibit a stronger tendency to form pairs. Additionally, our calculations reveal that manganese adatoms on a flat silicene surface introduce a new energy level within the bandgap of silicene, positioned closer to the conduction band, thereby enhancing charge carrier mobility. In contrast, our findings suggest that manganese adatoms on a buckled silicene surface introduce two separate energy levels within the bandgap, positioned equidistantly, thereby reducing charge carrier mobility. Overall, our study demonstrates that manganese adatoms on hexagonal boron nitride offer considerable potential for use in spintronics and other nanoscale devices. We also explore the feasibility of detecting these energy levels experimentally via scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Our study provides valuable insights into the design of spintronic devices based on silicene and other two-dimensional materials. We also discuss the potential applications of these devices in electronics and for quantum computing. We have found that the energy gap between the energy levels in manganese adatoms on a flat silicene surface can be tuned by adjusting either the substrate-substrate or the substrate-adatom distances. Furthermore, our calculations show that the energy levels in manganese adatoms on a buckled silicene surface are split into two distinct sublevels, one positioned closer to the Fermi level than the other. In contrast, our findings suggest that the energy levels in manganese adatoms on a flat silicene surface are split into two levels positioned equidistantly from the Fermi level. This paper introduces an original method for monitoring the thickness of thin polymer films through ellipsometry by lengthening the typical two-electrode setup to four electrodes, arranged in a specific configuration known as a Seiko M400 ellipsometer. By modulating the electron beam in a controlled manner, we obtain film thickness data over a broader detection range. Specifically, we employ a modulation period of 100 ns to measure thickness variations within a range of 10-150 Angstroms, utilizing a commercial Seiko M400 ellipsometer. This extended setup is particularly beneficial in analyzing the dynamic changes in polymer films, such as those undergoing relaxation, blending, or crosslinking processes, over extended periods. To illustrate the method's effectiveness, we provide three examples: (1) the study of poly(methyl methacrylate) films exhibiting thickness fluctuations, (2) the analysis of poly(styrene) and poly(methacrylate) blends, and (3) the observation of poly(methacrylate) films undergoing crosslinking reactions. In each case, we discover novel insights that could not be obtained using the conventional two-electrode setup. For instance, in polymer blends, we find that the thickness of individual layers is influenced by the surrounding films, leading to a more uniform blend composition. Furthermore, in crosslinking reactions, we find that the thickness of the films follows a specific exponential law, rather than a linear relationship as previously thought. These findings demonstrate the method's potential to provide a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics within thin polymer films, ultimately contributing to the development of innovative materials with unique properties. Although this study primarily focuses on polymer films, the method can be widely applicable to various systems, including biological membranes and nanomaterials. By combining lengthened ellipsometry with data analysis software, researchers can uncover new length-related physics in a broad range of materials. To facilitate the adoption of this technique, we provide a detailed guide on setting up and operating the four-electrode setup, along with a simple data analysis program, both of which are available for free. In conclusion, this study presents an original method for monitoring thin polymer films through ellipsometry, offering a range of benefits, including increased thickness detection precision, broader detection range, longer measurement periods, and more comprehensive thickness data analysis. Ultimately, this technique has the potential to provide a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics within thin polymer films, paving the way for the development of innovative materials with unique properties. A crucial mathematical innovation, the Riemann-Hilbert problem, underpins the creation of various transformation methods for resolving partial differential equations. Among these techniques, the outward complex scaling approach holds significant value in tackling non-relativistic Schrödinger equations, particularly in extreme electro-magnetic environments. This method entails shifting the coordinate system outward in a specific direction to eliminate unbounded boundary conditions. As a result, the time-dependent Schrödinger equation can be transformed into a coupled system of two first-order ordinary differential equations. This tutorial aims to provide a comprehensive review of the outward complex scaling approach, focusing on its application to atoms and molecules in intense direct current (DC) fields. A detailed explanation of this method will be provided, along with an examination of its applications, including systems with DC-paralleling and perpendicular fields. A thorough analysis of the approach's effectiveness and potential limitations in resolving one- and two-electron systems will be presented. Lastly, an assessment of the current state of the art and future research directions will be discussed. Although this review primarily focuses on the outward complex scaling approach, it also touches on other boundary condition strategies for resolving non-relativistic Schrödinger equations in extreme electro-magnetic environments. Additionally, a list of relevant references is included. Due to space constraints, this review primarily focuses on the application of the outward complex scaling approach; a companion paper will explore other boundary condition strategies for resolving non-relativistic Schrödinger equations. The companion paper will be published separately. The outward complex scaling approach has been successfully implemented in a software package, outward_complex_scaling.jl, which is now available on GitHub. This package can be easily integrated into Julia programming environments. A detailed user manual for this package is also provided. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to a significant increase in urban residents' stays at home, with corresponding changes in movement patterns. To investigate how income influenced urban interactions, a study analyzed the movement data of residents in Beijing, Shanghai, and Shenzhen from 2020 to 2021 using a socioeconomic classification system that groups residents into three income levels. Results show that lower-income individuals reduced their daily outings by 60% compared to higher-income residents during the pandemic, with a substantial proportion of their reduced outings targeting high-end destinations. Following the pandemic, high-income residents returned to their pre-pandemic frequency of leaving home, whereas low-income individuals continued to limit their daily outings, ultimately resulting in a more concentrated and segregated urban social environment. Notably, low-income individuals experienced increased visits to low-end public spaces such as parks and markets, while high-income residents predominantly avoided these areas. Income disparity in urban interactions was found to have intensified, with a notable disparity in the use of public spaces among different income groups. Income inequality in urban interactions was found to have been exacerbated, with lower-income individuals increasingly isolated from high-end destinations and higher-income residents avoiding public spaces frequented by lower-income individuals. often exhibit distinct brain activity patterns in the midbrain, a region
associated with prediction error processing, a critical component of adaptive
learning processes. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between
predictive error processing in the midbrain and the various strategies people
employ to learn, including both effective and less effective methods. By
analyzing task performance and brain activity using functional magnetic
resonance imaging, we discovered a correlation between midbrain activity and
the use of suboptimal reinforcement learning strategies, regardless of task
outcome. Furthermore, we found that effective learners tend to rely on a
characteristic type of learning strategy, which we term model-based learning.
These findings collectively suggest that midbrain prediction error processing is
integral to the development of efficient learning strategies. The results also
underscore the importance of considering the diverse range of learning
strategies, rather than solely focusing on optimal performance, when studying
reinforcement learning and brain function. Ultimately, this study highlights

We investigate the influence of electron spill-over and nonlocal effects on gap plasmons in the infinitesimal gap limit. Employing different electron models, including both local and nonlocal versions of the Random Phase Approximation, we calculate and compare dipole plasmon frequencies and decay rates, and find that nonlocal effects have a notable impact on these properties in the infinitesimal gap limit. The research also includes a discussion of the practical implications for experimental efforts to observe 3D-like gap plasmons in the vicinity of nanogaps. The research findings are further supported by computational simulations using Finite Elements. This research introduces an innovative approach to prejudice reduction in LiDAR scan matching by employing deep neural networks. Conventional scan matching algorithms often rely on a fixed, assumption-based prejudice for calculating continuous and discrete alignment errors. However, this prejudice can lead to suboptimal performance when assumptions are violated, causing prejudiced estimates of discrete registration errors. Real-world applications typically involve on-board perception for autonomous systems, which often encounter various and dynamic environments, exacerbating potential prejudice issues. To address this limitation, a deep neural network filter is proposed to modify existing scan matching outputs, mitigating prejudice without altering underlying algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in reducing prejudice error and outperforming other methods in complex and varied environmental settings. Moreover, the proposed method's simplicity enables seamless integration with existing LiDAR-based perception systems. Evaluation was conducted using a publicly accessible, diverse dataset from the ROSENL dataset collection. This contribution aims to enhance the robustness and adaptability of perception modules by minimizing prejudice, ultimately benefiting autonomous systems requiring on-board perception. Satellite images contain a wealth of information that can be accessed by deep networks with sufficient data, but they are also susceptible to changes in appearance due to variations in resolution and viewing angles. In an effort to prioritize interpretability, we aim to locate the edges of the Earth's surface in satellite images using only basic transformations and no complex networks. Our approach involves transforming raw images into a simplified representation by removing the background and normalizing the scale, effectively condensing the data into a set of edge points. This reduced representation enables us to pinpoint the edges of the Earth's surface via k-nearest-neighbor search, effectively replacing the need for a deep network. Our proposed method demonstrates a notable 30-fold reduction in parameter count, making it easier to interpret and understand. In addition, we have developed a comprehensive dataset containing 1,500 images, 500 of which are used for training, 500 for validation, and 500 for testing, all sourced from the OpenSatImagge benchmark. Our results show that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on this benchmark, achieving a mean absolute error of 0.88 degrees when tested on the full dataset. Furthermore, we have also demonstrated that our reduced representation can be used to successfully transfer knowledge to smaller models, achieving a mean absolute error of 1.13 degrees with a 30-fold reduction in parameters. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/krishnan-ucb/satellite-edge-identification. Our findings suggest that the reduced representation paradigm offers a viable compromise between interpretability and performance that is well-suited to transfer learning scenarios. In particular, our results show that our approach can be used to successfully transfer knowledge from large models to smaller ones, while also enabling the interpretation of the large model's behavior. Our paper presents the first comprehensive evaluation of the reduced representation paradigm in the context of satellite image edge identification, offering insights into its strengths and limitations. Traditional approaches to segmentation rely on manual evaluation, a time-consuming process prone to errors and subjective interpretation. Automated segmentation methods, though developed through large datasets of annotated images, often struggle with generalizability and those utilizing domain adaptation techniques may not fully address the issue. Given the significant variability in MS lesion appearance, learning-based approaches face significant challenges in adapting to new, unseen data. This paper investigates the application of online continual learning to mitigate the challenges in MS lesion segmentation, specifically exploring the efficacy of Incremental Maximum Likelihood Estimation (IMLE) in comparison to conventional training methods. Our findings indicate that models employing online continual learning, despite initial performance lags, demonstrate comparable or superior performance relative to those trained without such adaptation, as well as notable improvements in their ability to adapt to unseen data. This research provides an initial exploration into the application of online continual learning in MS lesion segmentation and highlights the need for further investigation into the potential of this approach in addressing the inherent challenges in this task. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/akanshgarg/Online-Continual-Learning-for-Multiple-Sclerosis-Segmentation. The authors also acknowledge the limitations of this study, including the absence of data augmentation and the use of a single dataset, and recommend future research incorporating diverse datasets and the application of data augmentation techniques to enhance the robustness of the models. Our findings suggest that online continual learning may offer a valuable approach in adapting deep learning models to segmentation tasks with limited data, and we anticipate that this research will contribute positively to the advancement of segmentation methods in the field of radiology. Dual comparison evaluates whether a function's dual has a non-differentiable concave segment, and this paper presents three conditions that are necessary and sufficient for dual comparison to occur. These conditions are related to the function's second and third derivatives on that segment. Additionally, the paper demonstrates how dual comparison conditions apply to specific monopsony models, such as the perfectly competitive inverse demand function, the uniform price model with a binding bid, and the posted-price model. In each of these models, the analysis reveals that dual comparison occurs when a particular, model-dependent threshold on the function's third derivative exceeds its second derivative. This finding implies that dual comparison depends on the level of labor supply in question. Furthermore, the paper examines how dual comparison affects the optimal and efficient quantity and wage outcomes for each of these models. While dual comparison does not impact the efficient quantity and wage in the perfectly competitive inverse demand and uniform price models, it does in the posted-price model. Recent studies on preference learning have shown that contextual preference models can improve preference inference by taking task-specific details into account. However, the effect of context on preference learning has not been thoroughly explored. This paper proposes a new task, set addition, which helps us understand how context affects preference learning. The set addition task involves learning how to combine two sets into a single, larger set based on given attributes and context. Three experimental tasks were designed to investigate context impact: set addition with various contexts, set addition with different attributes, and set addition without context. The results showed that our contextual model outperformed the non-contextual model across all tasks, indicating that context matters in set addition. Moreover, our study revealed that different context, rather than attributes, significantly affects learning performance. Overall, our research demonstrates the importance of context in set addition and highlights the need for further investigation of context impact on preference learning. The code for our study is available at https://github.com/kuo-chen-chen/set-addition.git. The data used in this research can be found at https://drive.google.

Our research introduces an innovative approach to address the vanishing gradient problem in denial-of-service scenarios in Transformer-based architectures. In denial-of-service attacks, the model continuously receives incorrect input, leading to catastrophic gradient updates. The newly proposed Denial Processing (DP) mechanism mitigates this issue by forcing the model to forget previous inputs on a per-sample basis during training. DP can be integrated with a wide range of existing transformer models with minimal modifications. Experimental results show that DP effectively solves the vanishing gradient issue, while outperforming state-of-the-art models in various benchmark tests, particularly in challenging denial-of-service attack scenarios. The approach also offers enhanced robustness and remains compatible with popular gradient descent optimizers. Development of DP is inspired by the concept of childhood amnesia, where humans naturally forget earlier experiences as they age. Building upon this idea, DP aims to replicate this forgetting mechanism in language models, effectively preventing the accumulation of past inputs. The implementation details of DP can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/your-profile/dp-transformer. Additionally, a pre-trained model based on the BART architecture is available through HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/dp-bart-large-cc. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel look-forward attention mechanism that only considers yet-to-be-produced target words as relevant history. Our proposed mechanism is compatible with a wide range of standard Transformer models and can be easily incorporated into existing NMT implementations. Experimental results demonstrate that this new attention mechanism leads to notable improvements in BLEU scores, with an average increase of 0.63 for standard Transformer models on the WMT19 translation task. Furthermore, our implementation is available at https://github.com/linxue/lfa. Our analysis suggests that the look-forward nature of this attention mechanism offers a more interpretable and semantically coherent form of production history. To illustrate this point, we conduct a case study using human-evaluated examples and find that the look-forward attention mechanism tends to avoid early inaccuracies, resulting in more natural and fluent translations. Our analysis also reveals that the look-forward attention mechanism can provide insights into its own decision-making process, potentially shedding light on its inner workings. Overall, our proposed mechanism is a versatile tool that can be used to enhance the robustness and transparency of NMT models through its novel form of production history. The versatility of this mechanism makes it an attractive candidate for a wide range of applications, including post-editing, translation assistance, and other related tasks. To further explore its potential, we conduct a series of additional experiments and find that the look-forward attention mechanism can be used to improve the quality of human-written translations. Our results indicate that the look-forward attention mechanism leads to notable increases in fluency and accuracy, with an average improvement of 0.43 and 0.25 in METEOR and BLEU4 metrics, respectively. Our analysis suggests that the look-forward attention mechanism can be used to provide translation systems with more forward-looking and robust production histories. Our analysis encompasses a broad range of interactions within the systems, with particular focus on how the shape of entanglement surfaces influences the results. In specific cases, we compare the entanglement entropy of large N gauge theories to the predictions made by black hole dualities in gravity models. Our findings reveal that, at large N, thermal and entanglement entropies exhibit a proportional relationship, with the proportionality constant being dependent on the size and shape of the entanglement surface. Notably, we find that this relationship holds true even for non-conformal field theories. In contrast, the case of boundary entanglement entropy does not follow this proportionality. Additionally, we explore the applicability of the Cardy formula for entanglement entropy in systems with varying degrees of non-Abelian symmetry. Our analysis indicates that while the formula accurately predicts the linearly proportional relationship between thermal and entanglement entropies, it fails to account for the dependence on the size of the subsystem. However, we observe that this dependence can be recovered by assuming the presence of a conformal fixed point at large N. Using this assumption, we derive a modified version of the Cardy formula that accurately predicts the entanglement entropy of large N gauge theories with non-Abelian symmetry. Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of the relationship between thermal and entanglement entropies in complex systems, with the large N limit serving as a useful benchmark for testing holographic duality across a wide range of interaction strengths. Furthermore, our analysis sheds light on the limitations of the Cardy formula, revealing that while it provides an accurate estimate of the linearly proportional relationship between thermal and entanglement entropies, it fails to account for certain non-linear corrections. These non-linear corrections are found to be dependent on the size of the subsystem and the strength of the interactions within the system. To gain a deeper understanding of how deep neural networks process images, researchers have been exploring ways to visualize the inner workings of these models. However, existing studies have primarily focused on the most active regions within the models, while neglecting the equally important contributions of other less active areas. In this research, we introduce the Hidden Visual-Semantic Filter Attention (HVSFA), a novel method for analyzing deep neural networks that prioritizes the less active regions, enabling us to identify and interpret the hidden features of these areas. By doing so, we can improve the accuracy of image classification by leveraging the collective insights from all regions. Our proposed method has been applied to multiple datasets, including CUB-200-2011 and Stanford Online Organism Dataset, and has achieved state-of-the-art results, with a notable accuracy of 71.0% on the CUB-200-2011 dataset. Our findings indicate that the less active regions of these models contain rich semantic information, and that by tapping into these hidden features, we can enhance our understanding of the visual-semantic processes underlying deep neural networks. Our code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/whswhs/HVSFA. Through this work, we hope to inspire future research to uncover the hidden strengths of these models. This study explores the exponential stability of a strongly continuous operator c0-semigroup on a Banach space and investigates the relationship between this stability and the robustness of the semigroup. A uniform robustness condition is established for the semigroup, and this condition can be satisfied if a certain Lyapunov equation has unique solutions. A nontrivial example of a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space demonstrates that the exponential stability of a semigroup does not necessarily imply the robustness of the semigroup. Additionally, this example highlights the necessity of a Lyapunov condition in establishing robustness. Furthermore, this study examines the relationship between the spectral radius Reg(f) of an operator f and the robustness of the semigroup generated by the sum of two operators, showing that robustness occurs when Reg(f) < 1. A nontrivial example of a bounded linear operator on an infinite-dimensional space demonstrates that the robustness of the semigroup can fail when Reg(f) equals 1. Finally, this study examines the relationship between the robustness of the semigroup and the stability of the time-dependent Cauchy problem within a Banach space and provides an example of a bounded linear operator on an infinite-dimensional space for which the time-dependent Cauchy problem is unstable. However, when the space is the space of bounded real-valued functions defined on a compact interval, this study establishes the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the time-dependent Cauchy problem and demonstrates the exponential stability of the solutions. A Lyapunov equation is used to establish the exponential stability of the solutions, and this example highlights the utility of a Lyapunov equation in establishing the stability of the time-dependent Cauchy problem within a Banach space. A new Monte Carlo event generator, KKMCee, has been developed to simulate hadron and lepton pair production through multi-photon processes in lepton colliders. The events generated by POLPHIee allow for the easy modeling of two-photon processes in lepton collider simulations. The development of these tools is expected to facilitate more accurate simulations of lepton colliders by incorporating the full physics of multi-photon processes. A robotic vision system consisting of an eye-in-hand camera can significantly
increase the accuracy of part-based object recognition by utilizing multiple views.
However, the high degree of freedom in eye-in-hand cameras makes it challenging
to identify objects of arbitrary shapes, as traditional methods often rely on
pre-existing 3D models or precise pose estimations, which are not feasible in
real-world applications where objects can have irregular shapes and ambiguity.
This paper proposes a novel deep learning approach that enables an end-effector to
automatically capture a 2D part view from an irregular 3D surface without any
need for pre-defined 3D models or pose estimations. By employing a single image
from a database of object parts, the approach adjusts the end-effector's position
and orientation. A simulation environment based on the Challenging Environment
Kit is used to test the proposed approach and compare it with existing methods. 
Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other
methods in both simulation and real-world experiments. The source code for this
approach can be accessed on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/

We investigate learning a function that reverses the behavior of a pre-existing policy. This policy is initially trained using reinforcement learning, utilizing a synthetic dataset. Our goal is for the reversed function to minimize interactions with the environment, akin to a mirror image of the original policy's behavior. To achieve this, a novel generative model is developed, incorporating constraints to preserve interactions from the original policy. Through experimentation, the efficacy of this approach is demonstrated, particularly in learning environment-invariant behaviors. A key advantage of our method lies in its ability to reverse policies with complex and high-dimensional action spaces, as illustrated through its application to playing Backgammon moves against a self-supervised opponent. Additionally, the proposed approach exhibits promising results in off-policy evaluation, enabling accurate estimation of the target return under specific conditions. Finally, the reversals generated by our method show potential in off-policy optimization, particularly when combined with other techniques such as imitation learning. Notably, the performance of our method is comparable to that of expert data when used as a reward function in imitation learning. This research opens up possibilities for future exploration in reverse function learning, potentially leading to applications in data efficiency, reward learning, and the discovery of natural inductive biases. A comprehensive implementation of the proposed method is available on GitHub, complete with supporting code and configuration files. Moreover, a web-based interactive platform has been developed to facilitate the exploration of reverse function learning, allowing users to input various policies and observe the generated functions using our approach. A key finding from this project is the emergence of "natural" functions when reversing policies, as demonstrated through the analysis of the generated functions in terms of their properties and behavior. To gain a deeper understanding of these results, a quantitative approach is employed to measure the similarity between the original and reversed functions, as well as their behavior in the environment. Interestingly, the properties of these functions appear to be transferable even when the reversal is not perfect, as evidenced by the fact that the reversed functions are able to compete with the original policy in the environment. This raises intriguing questions about the nature of these functions and their potential connection to more fundamental principles, as well as the potential applications of this research in fields such as transfer learning and multi-agent systems. Ultimately, the proposed method sheds light on the existence of inductive biases in learned behaviors and their potential exploitation through off-policy evaluation and optimization. A key limitation of this research is its reliance on pre-existing policies, as well as its current inability to handle continuous action spaces without the aid of additional techniques. Our proposed system, Box Re-Ranking (BRR), significantly reduces false positives in object detection by leveraging domain adaptation techniques and exploiting positive object interactions. BRR operates by re-evaluating detected objects within pre-defined bounding boxes, using an unsupervised learning approach that incorporates a combined loss function. This approach consists of two key components: 1) a domain adaptation method that adapapts a trained model to the target domain without the need for target domain annotations, and 2) a positive-negative box classification method. During training, BRR adapts to the target domain by learning an affinity matrix representing positive object interactions, and incorporates a supervised loss term based on valid annotations from the target domain. Meanwhile, it assigns an unsupervised loss term to negative boxes, thereby reducing false positives. Our experiments demonstrate that BRR achieves superior performance compared to existing domain adaptation and ranking techniques on the Citypersons dataset, resulting in an absolute mean average precision improvement of 1.1% and 0.9% for non-dominant and dominant individuals respectively. In the realm of machine learning, meta-learning focuses on developing algorithms that can learn other algorithms, often with the goal of improving performance on specific tasks.  This work introduces a new, straightforward framework for meta-learning, centered around a simple linear model.  This basic framework is capable of approximating more complex, non-linear methods, allowing for efficient learning on a wide range of tasks.  Our model, adaptable to various loss functions and data transformations, can handle diverse task characteristics.  Additionally, it is computationally efficient, scalable, and resilient to overfitting.  Experimental results confirm that it can learn and apply its findings effectively to unseen data sets.  Notably, our approach outperformed comparable methods in a benchmark test involving multi-digit image recognition.  Furthermore, we successfully applied it to a novel, more complex image recognition challenge where the model must learn to identify distortions in numerical patterns, without any explicit training on distortion handling.  Overall, our linear framework offers a versatile and efficient meta-learning solution, suitable for a broad range of tasks and data types.  Importantly, it is the first meta-learning method that can be learned and demonstrated by another algorithm, without any prior knowledge of the specific tasks at hand.  This work also highlights the importance of loss function design in achieving good performance and provides a theoretical understanding of the limitations and trade-offs involved in choosing an appropriate loss function.  Finally, our approach has potential applications in transfer learning and when access to task-specific data is limited.  The code for our method is publicly available and has been used to set new benchmarks in several image recognition challenges. This paper investigates the potential for reducing the computational and storage demands of neural machine translation models through quantization and pruning techniques. While previous studies have shown that these methods can significantly decrease the model's size and speed, they often overlook the critical issue of post-processing stability – the ability of the model to produce reliable outputs after quantization and pruning have been applied. To address this gap, we evaluated the impact of different quantization and pruning methods on the stability of an existing multilingual translation model using various metrics, including translation accuracy, word extraction, and semantic similarity. Our findings suggest that while quantization improves translation accuracy, it may not always enhance word extraction. Notably, pruning the model's final layer results in greater stability, but also reduces its ability to provide accurate translations. Accurate detection and measurement of the pleura and lungs in CT scans is crucial for diagnosing various lung conditions, including pneumonia. Lacking a comprehensive dataset for COVID-19 pneumonia, researchers often rely on existing datasets for testing segmentation models. However, compiling and labeling comprehensive datasets is resource-intensive and hinders the development of segmentation models. This study investigates whether image enhancement techniques can reduce the necessity for extensive labeling and produce more accurate segmentation results. We employed the Pneumonia-19 dataset, incorporating both COVID-19 and influenza pneumonia data, and utilized six distinct labeling approaches to develop U-Net-based models. Our experiments show that combining these techniques with standard training is on par with using full labels in terms of Dice score, while also demonstrating that incorporating influenza data does not hinder the models' performance. Furthermore, by leveraging these methods, we can achieve comparable results using 10% of the data required for traditional training, resulting in substantial training cost reductions. This finding suggests that image enhancement techniques can alleviate the limitations imposed by limited data availability and label resources. languages and speakers. Our experiments on a newly compiled dataset covering 11

even outperforms approaches that have access to pre-translated data. To the best
of our knowledge, zero-shot voice translation and the associated dataset
introduced in this research are firsts in the field of speech translation. Our
code is available at https://github.com/andreabacciu/zero-shot-voice-translation.

This process is characterized by the formation of electron currents that flow around magnetic islands, creating a force that drives island growth. In a new study, researchers have investigated how electron currents develop in slab plassemblies through both analytical calculations and simulations. They found that large-scale tearing modes cannot exist in collisionless plasmas due to an toepka rule, which is violated when finite temperatures are considered. Instead, the growth of tearing modes in both simulations and analytical calculations follows an exponential rate, similar to that predicted by the Floquet theorem. In contrast to large-scale modes, the growth of electron-scale tearing modes is slowed by the formation of electron currents that eventually saturate as islands form. This finding supports the idea that a sequence of small-scale tearing modes may be necessary to explain the rapid onset of full tearing modes in certain situations. Additionally, the study suggests that microscale tearing modes may be more difficult to trigger than large-scale modes, and that a critical threshold may exist below which these modes cannot exist in collisionless plasmas. To address the challenge of predicting areas that should be occluded, a model called the Occlusion-Aware Expense Creator (OACC) is developed. To improve the accuracy of predicted occlusion areas, OACC incorporates a refinement step using a channel-wise attention mechanism. Experiments using the standard 4-stage Lucas-Kanade algorithm on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, as it outperforms other methods even when their occlusion modules are disabled. Notably, our method's predicted occlusion areas can enhance the accuracy of Lucas-Kanade-based estimations by up to 2.5%, and also contribute to the generalization of other approaches.
